runs.report:
## Climate and Extreme Weather News: Past 30 Days

This report summarizes recent news regarding climate and extreme weather events, focusing on global impacts and policy responses, as reported within the last 30 days.

### Global Climate and Extreme Weather Events

*   **2024: A Record Warm Year & Unprecedented Extremes**
    *   2024 was the warmest year in 175 years of instrumental records, reaching 1.55°C above pre-industrial levels [source](https://www.arpafoundation.org/article/a-hotter-world-rewriting-rules-disaster).
    *   Unprecedented extreme weather displaced approximately 824,500 people, the highest in 16 years [source](https://www.arpafoundation.org/article/a-hotter-world-rewriting-rules-disaster).
    *   Global losses from natural catastrophes reached US$320 billion in 2024, with only US$140 billion insured; weather-related events were the primary contributors to these losses [source](https://www.arpafoundation.org/article/a-hotter-world-rewriting-rules-disaster).
    *   No single hazard dominated, with floods, cyclones, wildfires, and heatwaves occurring across multiple regions, highlighting interconnected climate risks driven by a warming ocean and atmosphere [source](https://www.arpafoundation.org/article/a-hotter-world-rewriting-rules-disaster).
*   **Annual Assessment of Weather and Climate Extremes (AWCE)**
    *   The first AWCE report from WCRP’s RIfS Global Extremes Platform (GEP) assesses 2025 extremes within a long-term context and a changing climate. It integrates extreme-event monitoring, long-term trends, event attribution, regional assessments, physical drivers, and detailed case studies [source](https://www.wcrp-climate.org/news/wcrp-news/2449-rifs-awce-1st-report).
*   **Natural Disaster Reporting Trends**
    *   Our World in Data presents an annual count of reported natural disaster events from 1900 to 2026. It notes that increases in reported events over time primarily reflect improved data reporting, rather than necessarily a real rise in disasters [source](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-natural-disaster-events).

### Policy Responses and Adaptation Efforts

*   **UK Launches Climate and Nature Security Taskforce**
    *   Britain has launched the world’s first Climate and Nature Security Taskforce to identify and address key climate- and nature-related security risks. Its objectives include identifying gaps, prioritizing risks, reviewing government work, and identifying opportunities to strengthen resilience and international influence [source](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/world-first-taskforce-to-protect-communities-from-climate-change).
    *   This initiative follows record heat, extreme weather, droughts, wildfires, and rising floods, highlighting climate risks to critical systems like energy, supply chains, and financial stability [source](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/world-first-taskforce-to-protect-communities-from-climate-change).
*   **EIB Doubles Climate Adaptation Funding**
    *   The European Investment Bank (EIB) will double its climate adaptation financing to at least €30 billion by 2030, prioritizing resilience for infrastructure, water, and agriculture [source](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/22/eib-to-double-climate-funding-to-30bn-as-extreme-weather-costs-soar).
    *   EIB President Nadia Calviño emphasizes that prevention is cost-effective, with each €1 invested in adaptation potentially saving €10 in damage and repairs [source](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/22/eib-to-double-climate-funding-to-30bn-as-extreme-weather-costs-soar).
    *   Extreme weather in 2025 caused €43 billion in EU losses, with projections suggesting €126 billion by 2029 [source](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/22/eib-to-double-climate-funding-to-30bn-as-extreme-weather-costs-soar).
*   **2026 Adaptation Forum Highlights Implementation**
    *   The 2026 Adaptation Forum (September 9–10, Baku) indicated a shift among countries from planning to implementing adaptation measures, with stronger systems to track results and learn from experience [source](https://unfccc.int/news/2026-adaptation-forum-highlights-practical-approaches-to-scaling-adaptation-implementation).
    *   Key findings include progress in national and local adaptation planning, but also gaps in predictable finance, sustained capacity, and reaching vulnerable communities [source](https://unfccc.int/news/2026-adaptation-forum-highlights-practical-approaches-to-scaling-adaptation-implementation).
    *   Emphasis was placed on coherent institutions, finance, and capacity aligned with local priorities, along with strengthened monitoring, learning, and forward-looking planning [source](https://unfccc.int/news/2026-adaptation-forum-highlights-practical-approaches-to-scaling-adaptation-implementation).
*   **Early Warning Systems**
    *   The number of countries with functioning early warning systems rose to 108 in 2024 (from 52 in 2015), under the UN’s Early Warnings for All initiative. However, roughly half of all countries, particularly the poorest and small island states, still lack adequate multi-hazard systems [source](https://www.arpafoundation.org/article/a-hotter-world-rewriting-rules-disaster).
    *   Recommendations include hyperlocal early warnings tailored to communities and the integration of indigenous knowledge with formal systems to enhance observation and resilience [source](https://www.arpafoundation.org/article/a-hotter-world-rewriting-rules-disaster).

## Global Climate and Extreme Weather Report: Past 30 Days

This report summarizes major climate and extreme weather events reported globally within the last 30 days, largely influenced by a strengthening El Niño.

### Global Climate Drivers and Outlook

*   **Strengthening El Niño**: The current El Niño is exceptionally strong, intensifying global extreme weather and is likely to persist through at least 2027 [bbc.com](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo), [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026), [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/tourist-attractions-shut-and-cattle-starving-how-el-nino-is-wreaking-havoc-around-the-worl). It is expected to peak by year-end and could be among the strongest on record [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/tourist-attractions-shut-and-cattle-starving-how-el-nino-is-wreaking-havoc-around-the-worl). El Niño's effects are amplified by human-caused warming [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/tourist-attractions-shut-and-cattle-starving-how-el-nino-is-wreaking-havoc-around-the-worl).
*   **Record Pacific Temperatures**: The UN/WMO warn of record Pacific temperatures and an unusually turbulent El Niño season [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/el-nino-rains-batter-latin-america-from-mexico-to-chile-4967563).
*   **Coral Reef Threat**: Coral reefs face heightened risk from heat and bleaching, with 44% of reef-building species threatened with extinction [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/tourist-attractions-shut-and-cattle-starving-how-el-nino-is-wreaking-havoc-around-the-worl).

Recent and forecasted rains raise flood risk in southern Ethiopia, parts of Somalia, southern Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, and east-central DRC [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026).
    *   **Drought/Dryness**: 90-day rainfall deficits are causing abnormal dryness and deteriorating vegetation in Chad, western Sudan, parts of South Sudan, northern Uganda, and parts of Ethiopia [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026). Abnormal dryness is also noted in central Mali, central/eastern Liberia, and southern Côte d’Ivoire due to prolonged below-average rainfall [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026).
    *   **Heat**: Abnormal heat is forecast in the eastern Sahel and parts of eastern/southern Africa [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026). Heat hotspots are forecast in southern Chad, northern/eastern Central African Republic, southern Sudan, South Sudan, Uganda, northwestern Kenya, and above-average temperatures in Zambia, Malawi, and central Mozambique [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026).
*   **Americas**:
    *   **Eastern Pacific Hurricane Season**: Unusually active with 22 named storms, 12 hurricanes (10 major), and rapid intensification events like Hurricane Polo due to very warm ocean waters [bbc.com](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo).
    *   **North Atlantic Hurricane Season**: Increased wind shear from El Niño restrained hurricane formation, with only one hurricane (Isaias) making landfall in the U.S. during the period [bbc.com](https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo).
    *   **U.S. Southwest**: A rare severe-weather outbreak brought tornadoes to central Arizona, damaging homes, trees, and causing power outages, and one injury [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/extreme-weather-tornado-hail-arizona-2fe815b7570812ad0f2cb4278379e185). Torrential flooding forced evacuations and state of emergency declarations in Utah and Colorado [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/extreme-weather-tornado-hail-arizona-2fe815b7570812ad0f2cb4278379e185).

        *   **Central America**: Severe droughts are notable in the Dry Corridor and El Salvador, leading to livestock losses [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/tourist-attractions-shut-and-cattle-starving-how-el-nino-is-wreaking-havoc-around-the-worl). Flood threats persist in Central America, Hispaniola, and Colombia [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/global-weather-hazards-summary-october-22-2026-october-28-2026).
        *   **Panama**: A magnitude 7.5 earthquake on October 9th affected over 35,000 people, with over 5,000 in shelters and significant housing damage [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/panama/panama-earthquake-azuero-veraguas-situation-report-no-06-21-october-2026-1330). Heavy rainfall and landslides pose an additional risk in affected districts [reliefweb.int](https://reliefweb.int/report/panama/panama-earthquake-azuero-veraguas-situation-report-no-06-21-october-2026-1330).
        *   **Paraguay**: Severe flooding along the Paraná River has affected approximately 4,200 families and caused two deaths [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/el-nino-rains-batter-latin-america-from-mexico-to-chile-4967563).
        *   **Argentina**: Two farm workers were killed near Bella Vista, and hundreds evacuated in Corrientes province due to flooding [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/el-nino-rains-batter-latin-america-from-mexico-to-chile-4967563).

Summary:
- Global heatwaves are starting earlier on land and lasting longer in a warming climate.
- From 1979–2023, heatwave onset advanced by about 3.29 days per decade, endings were delayed by about 5.41 days per decade, and heatwave seasons lengthened by about 8.71 days per decade.
- Timing changes covered large portions of global land: 72.0% for earlier onset, 79.6% for later ending, and 92.1% for longer season, with statistically significant trends across 13.4%, 20.3% and 34.4% respectively.
- A notable shift toward faster heatwave onset is observed in recent decades.
- Drylands show more pronounced timing shifts than humid regions.
- Implication: heatwave timing should be incorporated into early-warning systems, risk assessments, and proactive adaptation strategies under climate change.

Summary:
- 2024 set a global record for heavy precipitation frequency, defined as events at or above the 99th percentile (FP≥99), based on MSWEP data (1979–2025).
- Long-term trend: FP≥99 increases ~0.03% per decade; FP≥99.9 shows a similar but more uncertain rise.
- 2024 was unusually global in scope, with a distinct seasonal evolution and strong early-year drivers from El Niño and rare multi-basin tropical ocean warmth, followed by lagged tropospheric responses sustaining extremes through boreal summer.
- Model interpretation:
  - Years with 2024-like FP≥99 anomalies typically require stronger El Niño forcing or widespread basin-scale SST anomalies.
  - Constrained ensemble projections suggest ~40% of the 2024 anomaly aligns with higher global mean temperatures, ~20% with El Niño variability, and the rest with basin SST structure.
- FP≥99.9 (more extreme events) in 2024 reached 0.144% globally, a 44% increase over climatology, with high uncertainty due to limited historical events and observational sampling.
- Long-term FP≥99.9 trends in models exceed observed trends in some baselines; observed trends are within natural variability for three of four ensembles but are still subject to observational biases and internal variability.
- Takeaway: 2024’s spike reflects both a warming signal and favorable tropical SST configurations, highlighting that extreme precipitation is rising and can be amplified when ENSO and multi-basin SST patterns synchronize.
results.title: Record-setting heavy precipitation occurrence in 2024 | Science Advances

### Recent Scientific Reports and Analyses

*   **Global Heatwave Trends:** Global heatwaves are starting earlier and lasting longer, with significant shifts observed across a large portion of global land. From 1979–2023, heatwave onset advanced by approximately 3.29 days per decade, endings were delayed by 5.41 days per decade, and heatwave seasons lengthened by about 8.71 days per decade. These timing changes covered 72.0% for earlier onset, 79.6% for later ending, and 92.1% for longer seasons. Dryland regions exhibited more pronounced timing shifts [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-026-02762-2).
*   **Record Heavy Precipitation in 2024:** The year 2024 set a global record for the frequency of heavy precipitation events (at or above the 99th percentile), based on MSWEP data from 1979–2025. This unusually global scope had strong early-year drivers from El Niño and rare multi-basin tropical ocean warmth, followed by lagged tropospheric responses. Model interpretations suggest about 40% of the 2024 anomaly is linked to higher global mean temperatures and 20% to El Niño variability [science.org](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aeb1692).
*   **Advances in Extreme Event Attribution:** New research updates the IPCC AR6 regional synthesis figures for hot extremes, heavy precipitation, and agricultural/ecological drought. Key advances since 2021 include a doubling of extreme-event and attribution studies, enhanced methodologies, and a broadened evidence base for extremes on yearly to multiyear timescales. The authors advocate for regular updates to these visuals and broader hazard coverage for future assessments [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1088/2752-5295/aeaf75).

### Climate Data and Monitoring Initiatives

*   **Annual Assessment of Weather and Climate Extremes (AWCE):** The first AWCE report for the RIfS Global Extremes Platform (GEP) covers extremes observed in 2025. This report provides an integrated view, placing individual extreme events in their historical context and relating them to a changing climate, combining monitoring, trend analysis, attribution, and case studies [wcrp-climate.org](https://www.wcrp-climate.org/news/wcrp-news/2449-rifs-awce-1st-report).
*   **ERA5-EX Dataset for Extremes:** ERA5-EX is a new global 0.1-degree gridded dataset of temperature and precipitation extremes from 1950 to 2025, derived from ERA5-Land. It includes 34 annual variables, comprising 26 indices from the Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices and 8 bivariate (compound) metrics. The dataset supports climate monitoring and risk assessment with high-resolution, globally consistent extreme-event data and an accompanying processing toolkit [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-08312-x).
*   **Natural Disaster Event Reporting:** Our World in Data presents yearly counts of reported natural disaster events from EM-DAT (1900–2026). It's important to note that the long-term increase in reported events mainly reflects improvements in data reporting and collection rather than an actual rise in total disaster frequency. This data includes droughts, earthquakes, extreme temperatures, storms, floods, volcanic activity, and wildfires [ourworldindata.org](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-natural-disaster-events).

# Semiconductor Industry: Key Developments in the Past 30 Days

## Policy and Geopolitics

*   **U.S. Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) Expansion:** The Treasury Department issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to expand and update the OISP, aiming to curb U.S. outbound investments that could benefit foreign adversaries in key technology sectors like semiconductors, AI, and quantum information, while maintaining an open investment environment. The NPRM outlines requirements for notification and prohibition of certain transactions and seeks stakeholder feedback [source](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0667/).
*   **Strengthening U.S. AI Chip Export Controls:** Proposals in the U.S. advocate for stronger AI chip export controls, including location verification on advanced AI chips, aligning allies' export controls with U.S. standards, and codifying existing restrictions into law through acts like the Chip Security Act, MATCH Act, and AI OVERWATCH Act [source](https://www.banks.senate.gov/news/in-the-news/strengthening-americas-ai-chip-export-controls/).
*   **Export Controls and Geopolitics Driving Access:** Access to advanced AI chips is increasingly determined by geopolitics rather than price, with export controls shaping who can receive restricted processors. A Taiwan case involving alleged smuggling of Nvidia AI servers highlights how compliance, verification, and supply-chain governance are critical as government approvals and international trust now dictate access [source](https://www.imd.org/ibyimd/geopolitics/the-long-way-to-china-what-chip-smuggling-reveals-about-trade-today/).
*   **Ongoing U.S. Export Controls:** U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors and computing items remain crucial for AI infrastructure projects, with recent developments including targeted changes affecting China's access to advanced chips and challenges with restricted parties accessing computing power remotely in third-country data centers [source](https://www.blankrome.com/news-and-events/whats-the-latest-with-semiconductor-export-controls/).

## Major Investments and Capacity Expansion

*   **GlobalFoundries U.S.-Japan $21B Initiative:** GlobalFoundries (GF) has been selected as the technology provider and operator for two new 300mm fabs in Malta, NY, with up to $21 billion in funding. The first line is expected online in 2029, with the U.S. Commerce Department reallocating up to $955 million for silicon photonics, SiGe, and advanced packaging [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly), [source](https://en.edaily.co.kr/news/eda202610165604/).
*   **GF and TSMC Collaboration for U.S. Supply:** GlobalFoundries announced a multi-year, $2 billion manufacturing agreement with TSMC to establish a U.S.-based supply of silicon interposers for TSMC's CoWoS advanced packaging ecosystem, with volume production ramping in H1 2028 at its Malta, NY facility [source](https://investors.gf.com/news-releases/news-release-details/globalfoundries-reaches-agreement-establish-us-based-supply).
*   **TSMC U.S. Expansion:** TSMC is accelerating its U.S. expansion, assessing a potential Texas plant and expanding its Arizona capacity with a $265 billion program for AI/HPC wafers and advanced packaging. A second Arizona factory is set to begin mass production in Q3 next year [source](https://en.edaily.co.kr/news/eda202610165604/).
*   **Samsung Taylor Plant Expansion:** Samsung Electronics' Taylor plant expansion is progressing, aiming for full operations soon and mass production by 2030, leveraging Tesla as a customer for AI/HPC and 2nm processes [source](https://en.edaily.co.kr/news/eda202610165604/).
*   **VSMC Singapore Fab Opening:** VSMC opened a US$7.8 billion 300mm fab in Singapore, targeting 55,000 wafers/month by 2029 for mixed-signal, power-management, analog, and interposer markets [source](https://greyradius.com/insights/newsletters/the-wafer/semiconductor-intelligence-sep28-oct4-2026/).
*   **Samsung Electro-Mechanics AI FC-BGA Investment:** Samsung Electro-Mechanics committed approximately US$5 billion to expand AI FC-BGA substrate production in Vietnam and Sejong, with mass production expected by September 2028 [source](https://greyradius.com/insights/newsletters/the-wafer/semiconductor-intelligence-sep28-oct4-2026/).
*   **TOPPAN–Broadcom FC-BGA Factory:** TOPPAN and Broadcom opened a high-end FC-BGA substrate factory in Singapore with an initial investment of S$405 million, targeting high-volume production by late 2026 [source](https://greyradius.com/insights/newsletters/the-wafer/semiconductor-intelligence-sep28-oct4-2026/).
*   **Applied Materials EPIC Center:** Applied Materials opened a $5 billion EPIC (Electronics Packaging Innovation Center) center and deepened its memory technology partnership with KIOXIA for next-gen memory cells [source](https://greyradius.com/insights/newsletters/the-wafer/semiconductor-intelligence-sep28-oct4-2026/), [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).

## Market Trends and Forecasts

*   **Significant Market Growth Forecasted:** The global semiconductor market is forecasted to grow from USD 1,655.00 billion in 2026 to USD 3,142.18 billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 8.3%. Other forecasts predict the market reaching USD 1,033.1 billion in 2026 and USD 3,128.7 billion by 2035 with a CAGR of ~14.9% [source](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/semiconductor-market-102365), [source](https://www.businessresearchinsights.com/market-reports/semiconductor-market-117565).
*   **AI and Data Centers as Key Drivers:** AI, generative AI, data center expansion, and high-performance computing are primary growth drivers, fueling demand for AI processors, GPUs, HBM, and networking chips [source](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/semiconductor-market-102365), [source](https://www.techinsights.com/outlook-reports-2026/semiconductor-outlook-report).
*   **Memory Price Spikes and Revenue:** Memory volatility is significantly influencing profits, with memory growing 302% in 2026 according to WSTS, outpacing other segments and heavily influencing overall industry revenue [source](https://srfcapital.studio/resources/articles/semiconductor-industry-analysis). Micron reported Q4 FY2026 revenue of US$54.23 billion with a tightening outlook for memory demand/supply in 2027-28 [source](https://greyradius.com/insights/newsletters/the-wafer/semiconductor-intelligence-sep28-oct4-2026/).
*   **Rising Fab Equipment Spending:** SEMI projects 300mm fab equipment spending to reach $227 billion by 2029, reflecting rapid fab expansion and strong capital expenditure for front-end fabs [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/), [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **Advanced Packaging and Photonics:** Silicon photonics and co-packaged optics (CPO) are anticipated to drastically reduce networking power (up to 70%) and boost data transfer speeds, with increasing thermal co-design and co-simulation efforts [source](https://www.techinsights.com/outlook-reports-2026/semiconductor-outlook-report), [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **Shift to 2nm Process Nodes:** A shift to 2nm process nodes is expected to deliver better power efficiency and higher performance, reshaping the foundry market [source](https://www.techinsights.com/outlook-reports-2026/semiconductor-outlook-report).
*   **HBM4 Memory Recovery:** Volume production of 16-Hi HBM4 is anticipated in H1 2026, driven by leading HBM suppliers advancing HBM3E to support AI chip demand [source](https://www.techinsights.com/outlook-reports-2026/semiconductor-outlook-report).
*   **Automotive and Defense Impact:** EVs, connected vehicles, and defense systems (radar, secure comms, EW) are boosting demand for power semiconductors, microcontrollers, sensors, and radiation-tolerant components, with military/aerospace defense being the largest segment at 57% of the market [source](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/semiconductor-market-102365), [source](https://www.businessresearchinsights.com/market-reports/semiconductor-market-117565).
*   **Profit Concentration and Supply Chain:** Profitability remains concentrated in high-entry-barrier areas like design platforms, leading-edge foundries, and lithography tools, with TSMC dominating the foundry market (72–73% share in mid-2026) and about 90% of advanced chip output attributed to Taiwan [source](https://srfcapital.studio/resources/articles/semiconductor-industry-analysis).

## Technology and Innovation

*   **AI-defined Fab Partnerships:** NVIDIA is forming AI-defined fab partnerships across the equipment and EDA ecosystem, positioning itself as both a customer and a manufacturing infrastructure provider [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **Advances in Lithography:** Imec is advancing lithography via AI/accelerated computing, and Nikon has introduced an advanced packaging lithography system [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly), [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **Thermal Co-design Emphasis:** Thermal management is a growing constraint, leading to increasing thermal co-design and co-simulation efforts, including co-packaged optics [source](https://www.originbrief.app/en/reports/semiconductor-chip-industry/2026-10-19/weekly).
*   **SiC Power Technology:** Infineon and Eaton are collaborating on SiC power technology for 800V DC AI data centers [source](https://greyradius.com/insights/newsletters/the-wafer/semiconductor-intelligence-sep28-oct4-2026/).
*   **Next-Gen Transistors and Memory:** Leading players like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are driving progress in high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging, with ongoing technology advances across memory, EUV, and packaging [source](https://www.businessresearchinsights.com/market-reports/semiconductor-market-117565), [source](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/).
*   **3D Integration for AI Chips:** Senior executives from TSMC, Intel, and Samsung discussed the critical role of advancing semiconductor processes and 3D integration to overcome barriers in AI chip development [source](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261013PD240/intel-tsmc-samsung-technology-development.html).
*   **Quantum Leadership:** GlobalFoundries received a $375 million U.S. Commerce Department R&D award to advance American quantum leadership [source](https://investors.gf.com/investor-relations/news-events/press-releases).

TSMC is accelerating U.S. expansion, including a Texas assessment after discussions with major U.S. customers seeking local production to diversify supply chains and reduce geopolitical risk. TSMC is already expanding Arizona capacity with a $265B program, aiming to cover wafers for AI/HPC, advanced packaging, and R&D, with a second factory set to begin mass production in Q3 next year. TSMC is also in talks with TerraFab (Tesla-led) about a potential plant, though details remain undecided.

Meanwhile, U.S. funding and localization efforts are increasing:
- The U.S. government, using Japanese investment funds, will invest about $21B into two GF-related semiconductor factories in Malta, NY (first plant starting 2029; 100% Japanese funds invested in U.S. manufacturing infrastructure).
- These moves aim to secure domestic supply, support American equipment makers, and bolster long-term plant operations and technology provision revenue (20-year horizon noted).

Industry competition dynamics:
- Samsung Electronics’ Taylor plant expansion is a focal point as competition tightens; its Taylor Plant 1 is moving toward full operations soon, targeting 2030 mass production, and leveraging Tesla as a customer for AI/HPC exposure and 2nm processes.
- Tesla-related orders (e.g., AI chips) and long-term supply contracts are expected to be key variables for stability in the U.S. foundry market.

Impact on memory players (SamsungElectronics, SK hynix) and U.S. foundry demand:
- Growing U.S. demand for local production could pressure existing players to scale U.S. facilities and adjust timelines for new plants.

results.search_result:
Summary of essential results

- Main question: Do geoeconomic shocks from export controls disrupt international production networks or cause reconfiguration of global value chains (GVCs)?
- Case study: October 2022 U.S. export controls on advanced computing and semiconductor technologies directed at China.
- Data and method: Bilateral product-level trade data for 44 exporters and 226 importers (2012–2024); analyzed with Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) gravity models to identify four propagation margins: 
  1) direct trade destruction
  2) supplier substitution
  3) geographic trade reallocation
  4) changes in product composition
- Key findings:
  - Reconfiguration over uniform destruction: U.S. semiconductor exports to China decline in value, especially in integrated circuits, but other countries (notably Japan and the Netherlands) increase exports to China in adjacent areas like semiconductor manufacturing machinery.
  - Shifting hubs: Semiconductor trade gravitates toward alternative production and assembly hubs, with heterogeneous responses across destinations and exporters.
  - Compositional adjustment: Within continuing trade relationships, there are changes in product mix and unit values, indicating quality/variant substitutions rather than a simple volume decline.
  - Transmission channels: Outcomes depend on technological specialization, substitutability among suppliers, and third-country absorption capacity; rivals the direct bilateral effect by creating broader network adjustments.
- Interpretation: The technology restriction shock does not simply shrink trade with China; it triggers a reallocation and realignment of global semiconductor trade, influencing how supply chains are organized and which countries become new nodes in production networks.
- Implications: Geoeconomic risk from export controls can reshape global production and transmit disturbances through reconfigured trade links, not solely by eliminating imports from targeted partners.
results.title: Geoeconomic Risk and the Reconfiguration of Global Semiconductor Trade: Evidence from U.S. Export Controls on China by Hong Ngoc Bui, Nandu Sasidharan :: SSRN

Key findings from “Who is most exposed to a chip supply shock?” (Samaritan Research):

- China is more exposed than the US to semiconductor supply disruptions. In 2022, Chinese final demand generated $15.2 in semiconductor revenue per $1,000 of demand, about 2.7× the $5.7 for the US.
- In a combined shock (Taiwan disruption plus China–West decoupling), China suffers much larger impacts: advanced processor prices rise about 17× in China, while the US sees roughly a 20% price increase; Chinese real GNE falls ~3% (potentially ~1% with narrower decoupling), versus ~0.6% for the US (or near-zero in the narrower scenario).
- Across robustness checks, China’s exposure and estimated losses consistently exceed the US, though exact magnitudes vary. Sensitivity drivers include how easily buyers switch between countries’ goods and how available substitutes are for processors.
- China’s exposure isn’t limited to its own demand: Chinese final demand also generates far more revenue for semiconductor industries in Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan than US demand does for those industries.
- Policy-relevant caveats: the model captures one channel (goods scarcity and price rise with supplier switching) over 2–3 years. It omits potential recession effects, financial sanctions, capital flight, firm-level bottlenecks, and chip inventories, which could amplify or cushion outcomes. The results should be read as the trade-channel impact of a disruption in a 2–3 year horizon.
- Additional note: using OECD ICIO (2024) data suggests China’s final-demand exposure to the global semiconductor industry could be lower (2.2× vs. 2.8× previously), modestly reducing the predicted GNE losses, but directionally similar—China remains more exposed than the US. Upcoming data updates are prioritized.

    *   Super Micro Computer guided Q1 revenue to $18.5B–$19.5B, well above prior guidance, due to favorable AI server demand mix. [vlsi.kr](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-22-en/)
    *   Samsung Electronics and SK hynix stocks rebounded, and Korea's Oct 1–20 semiconductor exports hit a record $27.5 billion, strongly contributing to AI-related demand. [vlsi.kr](https://www.vlsi.kr/en/daily-silicon-2026-10-22-en/)
    *   Over $8.5 billion in Q3 chip-industry startup funding was secured across ~80 companies, with a focus on AI inference, memory alternatives, and photonics. [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-160/)

### Geopolitical Impact and Supply Chain Resilience

Geopolitical tensions continue to reshape the global semiconductor supply chain, emphasizing the need for diversification and resilience.

*   **Reconfiguration of Supply Chains:**
    *   U.S. export controls on advanced computing and semiconductor technologies targeting China have led to a reconfiguration rather than uniform destruction of trade. While U.S. semiconductor exports to China declined, other countries like Japan and the Netherlands increased exports of manufacturing machinery to China. [papers.ssrn.com](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/7587799.pdf?abstractid=7587799&mirid=1)

[samaritan-research.org](https://samaritan-research.org/publications/china-us-semiconductor-supply-chain-exposure)
    *   U.S. semiconductor supply chains rely on a globally distributed network, with critical risks often lying deep in subtier networks (e.g., critical minerals). [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/semiconductors/our-insights/strengthening-supply-chains-behind-us-semiconductors)

*   **Policy and Resilience Strategies:**
    *   Strengthening supply chain resilience requires expanding domestic capacity, improving inventory management, securing supply chains, fostering international partnerships, and investing in R&D. [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/semiconductors/our-insights/strengthening-supply-chains-behind-us-semiconductors)
    *   Rising geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions create macroeconomic risks, but strong substitution, inventory use, and flexible production can help mitigate output losses, albeit at higher input prices. Lam Research and peers posted mixed results as earnings season kicked off.

- Lam Research: Q September revenue $8.22B, up 22% QoQ and ~54% YoY; GAAP EPS $2.19, non-GAAP $2.20. Guidance for Dec quarter: revenue $8.60B ±$400M; gross margin ~52.5%; operating margin ~40.5%. Stock finished down after the report.
- Nvidia (Vera Rubin): Vera Rubin platform in full production; DSX reference designs and cooling/efficiency benefits highlighted; Google Cloud to offer Vera Rubin-based A5X in November.
- Super Micro Computer: Q1 revenue guided to $18.5B–$19.5B, well above prior guidance; higher gross margin guidance (12.0%–12.5%) due to favorable AI server demand mix.
- Samsung Electronics and SK hynix: Both stocks rebounded (~+5.6% and +5.8%); Korea’s Oct 1–20 semiconductor exports hit a record $27.5B, with a strong contribution from AI-related demand.
- Korea export context: Oct 1–20 total exports up sharply year over year; semiconductor exports reached a record share of total exports.

Bottom line: Early chip-earnings results skew positive on demand for AI infrastructure and server workloads, with Lam seeing record quarterly revenue but a modest after-hours dip, Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform advancing, and Super Micro signaling robust AI-driven server demand. Korea export data underscored a strong AI-related semiconductor push.

Summary:
- The McKinsey–SIA collaboration maps US semiconductor upstream supply chains and identifies hidden vulnerabilities beyond Tier 1 suppliers, spanning global subtier networks.
- Key findings:
  1) Semiconductor manufacturing relies on a precisely coordinated flow of specialized materials and equipment from Tier 1 and subtier suppliers worldwide.

 3) No single fix suffices. Strengthening resilience requires a mix of actions: expanding domestic capacity, improved inventory management, secure and diversified supply chains, robust international partnerships, and sustained R&D in materials science, engineering, and recycling to reduce dependence on vulnerable inputs.
- Implication: Proactive, coordinated, long-term measures are needed now to protect future semiconductor investments and mitigate decades-long risk of disruptions.

Summary:

- The U.S. semiconductor supply chain is multi-tiered and globally dispersed; manufacturing inputs (equipment, materials) come from a mix of U.S., Europe, and Japan-based suppliers, but their supply chains span multiple countries.
- Many Tier 1 inputs depend on sub-tier materials and components with elevated disruption risk, creating hidden vulnerabilities deep in upstream supply chains.
- The report identifies critical materials and equipment categories used in U.S. semiconductor production and highlights vulnerabilities at risk of disruption.
- Key findings and recommended actions:
  - Onshoring and stockpiling: Focus on expanding domestic production and strategic inventories for feasible inputs; full onshoring of all inputs is impractical.
  - Allied supply chains: Strengthen and diversify supply chains with allied and partner nations to boost resilience.
  - Reduce dependence on unreliable sources: Expand U.S. and partner country mining and processing capacity for critical minerals; pursue long-term offtake agreements to sustain demand for new capacity.
  - Invest in R&D: Increase funding for materials science, chemistry, and engineering to develop new semiconductor materials and recycling technologies.
- Resilience approach: Building trusted supply chains requires sustained coordination among government, industry, and international partners.
- Vulnerability assessment (Tier 1): About half of analyzed supply categories show high (11%) or medium (38%) vulnerabilities, due to geographic concentration, narrow qualified supplier bases, or exposure to high-risk countries.

## Semiconductor Industry Report: October 2026

This report summarizes key developments in the semiconductor industry over the past 30 days, categorized for clarity. The overarching theme is robust growth driven by AI demand, leading to significant investments in manufacturing capacity, R&D, and strategic supply chain initiatives.

### **I. Company Announcements and Financial Performance**

The past month has seen major companies announcing significant investments and reporting strong financial results, largely fueled by the burgeoning AI market.

*   **NVIDIA**
    *   Announced plans to expand semiconductor manufacturing capacity due to high AI demand. This involves multi-year agreements with various suppliers to boost capacity for key components like substrates, advanced packaging, testing, and optical engines. [source](https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-today-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-10-21-2026/card/S8kOVoeKXiwOVNvmToNv), [source](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-supply-chain-partners-expand-capacity-to-accelerate-ai-infrastructure-buildout)

[source](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/semiconductors/our-insights/strengthening-supply-chains-behind-us-semiconductors), [source](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/mapping-the-semiconductor-value-chain_4154cdbf-en.html)

results.search_result:
Summary:
- Study compares PostgreSQL and MySQL performance using a benchmarking framework focused on continuous authentication with large-scale behavioral data.
- Key findings:
  - Select operations:
    - Fetching all records (1 million): PostgreSQL 0.6–0.8 ms vs. MySQL 9–12 ms (≈13× faster for PostgreSQL).
    - Select with where clause (e.g., uname = 'clair', ~10k rows from 1M): PostgreSQL 0.09–0.13 ms vs. MySQL 0.9–1 ms (≈9× faster for PostgreSQL).
    - Across all select statistics (median, min, max, percentiles), PostgreSQL consistently outperforms MySQL by about a factor of 13 in the reported results.
  - Insert operations:
    - Inserts over multiple trials: PostgreSQL 0.0007–0.0014 ms; MySQL 0.0010–0.0030 ms. Overall, performance is similar with PostgreSQL slightly better.
  - Complex/concurrent workloads:
    - Under simultaneous select/insert scenarios, PostgreSQL remains stable (≈0.7–0.9 ms for selects during inserts); MySQL degrades significantly (≈7–13 ms).
- Conclusion: PostgreSQL is more suitable for continuous authentication systems requiring low data latency and robust concurrent processing, due to superior select performance (with and without conditions) and more stable behavior under concurrent load.

Summary:
- This work presents a reproducible benchmark toolset and experimental design for comparing relational database access layers in an Express.js service, specifically PostgreSQL vs. MySQL, across multiple engines, configurations, and workloads.
- The benchmark covers native drivers and access patterns such as point reads, keyset range scans, deep/nested fetches, aggregations, and multi-statement transactions (including inserts and multi-row writes). It measures throughput (requests per second) and tail latency (p50, p90, p97.5, p99) under controlled conditions.
- Over revisions (v1.2 to v1.4), the study introduces rigorous statistical analysis (paired tests, Wilcoxon, TOST, paired p-values), CPU/resource accounting, and multiple targeted experiments:
  - Connection-pool size sensitivity
  - Single-host resource isolation
  - Transactional multi-statement write workloads
  - Multi-worker (node cluster) setups showing native drivers overtaking ORM layers when cores are fully utilized
  - Per-layer pool-size frontiers and mixed read/write workloads
  - Longer-run sensitivity checks and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all throughput results
  - Open-loop and closed-loop tail analyses with controlled utilization to examine saturated tails
- The findings emphasize configuration-specific performance determinants rather than a universal ranking. Key takeaways include:
  - Under matched utilization and tested configurations, native drivers may outperform ORM layers in certain patterns, especially when CPU cores are fully utilized.
  - The saturated tail (p99) is heavily influenced by workload mix, concurrency, and resource isolation; tail behavior stabilizes under matched utilization in some experiments but can diverge under others depending on the layer and workload.
  - The deep-fetch performance characteristics are consistent in relative terms across experiments, but the absolute growth pattern was clarified to be a roughly fixed multiplier with respect to graph size rather than a continuously growing factor.
- The work provides a replication package with the benchmark harness, paper sources, results, and an online supplement (Tables S1–S26) for detailed methodology, control settings, and statistical analyses.

If you want, I can tailor this to your exact query (e.g., PostgreSQL vs MySQL relative performance on specific patterns like point reads vs. deep fetch, or summarize the key numeric results from the supplement).

- Focus: Write-heavy sysbench tests on a large server comparing modern Postgres (versions 16.13, 17.9, 18.3, 19 beta1) vs MySQL 8.4.7 (InnoDB).
- Throughput and variance:
  - Postgres shows substantial throughput variance across tests.
  - InnoDB generally achieves higher average throughput than Postgres in 6 of 10 tests; similar in 1 test; Postgres outperforms InnoDB in 3 of 10 tests.
- Key per-operation observations:
  - Postgres tends to write more IO per operation (KB written) than InnoDB in tests like update-index and update-zipf.
  - InnoDB often uses more CPU and more context switches; autonomic vacuum activity is involved, but measurements exclude manual vacuums.
- Specific results by test type:

  - update-zipf: InnoDB ~1.09x Avg throughput vs Postgres; Postgres writes more IO per op; InnoDB uses more CPU.
  - insert: Postgres ~2.06x higher throughput than InnoDB; Postgres also writes more IO per op.
- IO/CPU patterns:
  - iostat/vmstat show Postgres and MySQL differences in IO and CPU usage per operation, with Postgres often heavier on write IO and CPU in some tests, and MySQL showing different patterns in others.
- Overall takeaway:
  - Throughput trends indicate potential regressions or overheads in newer Postgres builds (not conclusively proven) and a relative strength in InnoDB for several tests, particularly in write-heavy scenarios. The results also highlight higher variance for Postgres across the tested workloads.

results.search_result:
Essential results:

- PostgreSQL vs MySQL (InnoDB) are both mature, ACID-relational DBs suitable for web apps; choose based on architectural differences and ecosystem needs.
- When to pick PostgreSQL (default recommendation):
  - No constraints: PostgreSQL offers richer type system, more index options (partial, expression, GiST/GIN/BRIN), transactional DDL, full JSONB support, and extensive extensions.
  - You want built-in extensibility and advanced features in one database.
- When to pick MySQL (InnoDB):
  - Your team already operates MySQL well; operational competence matters.
  - Workload is dominated by primary-key lookups and simple writes; InnoDB’s clustered index and in-place updates suit high-volume PK workloads.
  - You want vendor-provided automatic failover (InnoDB Cluster) or you rely on Vitess sharding ecosystem.
- Replication and availability:
  - PostgreSQL: physical streaming replication (WAL) and logical replication; standby reads; hybrid upgrades across major versions possible with logical replication (but DDL not replicated in logical).
  - MySQL: binary log with GTIDs; Group Replication; built-in automatic failover.
- DDL and transactions:
  - PostgreSQL: most DDL is transactional and rollbacks are supported.
  - MySQL: each DDL statement is atomic with implicit commits.
- Sharding/Scaling paths:
  - PostgreSQL: Citus for sharding.
  - MySQL: Vitess for sharding.
- Other quick contrasts:
  - Connection model: PostgreSQL uses a process per connection; MySQL uses a thread per connection.
  - Storage: PostgreSQL stores rows in a heap with pointers from all indexes; MySQL uses a clustered B-tree on primary key with secondary indexes pointing to keys.
  - Isolation default: PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED; MySQL REPEATABLE READ.
  - Materialized views: PostgreSQL yes; MySQL no.

Bottom line guidance:
- If starting fresh: PostgreSQL is often the better all-in-one choice due to DDL transactional support, richer data types, and broader index/extension options.
- If you already run MySQL well or need built-in failover and easy sharding with Vitess, MySQL/InnoDB is compelling.

results.search_result:
Summary:
- PostgreSQL 18: Best for new apps or those needing strong features (Migrations with complete rollback, JSON indexes, extensions like pgvector, PostGIS, Swedish full-text search). Uses the least idle memory and restores dumps fastest (5–8x faster in their tests). Reads slower than MySQL/MariaDB but writes are on par with MariaDB. Disk size reasonable. Weak points: slower reads, single active process per connection; may require connection pooling (PgBouncer) and routine VACUUM.
- MySQL 9.7: Fastest for reads in the benchmark. Binary log (on by default) enables point-in-time recovery but hurts write speed and dump restores. Large image size and heavier initial memory footprint. DDL cannot be rolled back. Strong compatibility with PHP apps (e.g., WordPress).
- MariaDB 12.3: Similar to MySQL in behavior and app use-case; smaller image than MySQL, built‑in vector search, RETURNING and sequences, and mariadb-backup tool included. Writes were as fast as PostgreSQL in the tests. Shares MySQL’s DDL drawback and JSON storage as text, but has lower idle memory than MySQL and supports built-in vector features.

Bottom line guidance:
- Choose PostgreSQL for new apps needing advanced features, best dump/restore performance, and lower idle memory.
- Choose MySQL for PHP-focused apps needing fast reads and straightforward tooling, accepting potential write-speed cost from binary logging and limited rollback for DDL.
- Choose MariaDB for similar use-cases as MySQL but with a smaller image, built-in vector/search features, and comparable write performance to PostgreSQL.

Summary of essential results:

- Both PostgreSQL and MySQL scale to very large workloads in real-company stories.
- Notable examples:
  - PostgreSQL: OpenAI runs ChatGPT on a single primary with ~50 read replicas; Figma and Notion shard PostgreSQL themselves (custom query proxy and logical shards).
  - MySQL: GitHub handles 5.5 million QPS across 50+ clusters; Slack 2.3 million QPS; Shopify’s Shop app uses Vitess sharding; Meta’s TAO caches a graph stored in sharded MySQL.
- Scaling toolkit differences:
  - PostgreSQL stories rely on PgBouncer, read replicas, caching, and application-layer sharding (often custom).
  - MySQL stories frequently use Vitess for sharding, plus horizontal sharding, caching, and online migrations.
- Notable metrics and anecdotes:
  - OpenAI: 800 million users; 350 TB+ data; reads offloaded to replicas; writes handled with shardable approaches.
  - Canva: hundreds of millions of users; practical sharding/caching strategies reduce load; reduces read replicas via careful data handling.
  - Shopify: up to 5.5 million QPS on GitHub-scale workloads; inventory reservations use MySQL with selective locking strategies and online migrations.
  - TAO: Facebook’s graph cache over sharded MySQL delivering over a billion reads per second.
- Verdict: No clear winner by limits; success depends on tooling and architecture. MySQL teams lean on Vitess for sharding; PostgreSQL teams use PgBouncer, read replicas, caching, and custom/sharded approaches within applications.
- Sharding approaches:
  - PostgreSQL: custom proxy, logical sharding, and replication strategies.
  - MySQL: Vitess-based sharding and, in some cases, online/offline migration tools (e.g., Ghostferry).

runs.report:
## PostgreSQL vs. MySQL for Write-Heavy Web Applications

This report compares PostgreSQL and MySQL, specifically for write-heavy web applications, drawing from recent benchmarks, feature comparisons, and real-world scalability examples.

### Performance Benchmarks

Recent studies offer varying perspectives on performance, highlighting the importance of specific workloads and configurations.

*   **Mixed Workloads (Selects & Inserts)**
    *   A study focusing on continuous authentication found PostgreSQL significantly faster (13x for fetching all records, 9x for specific `WHERE` clauses) for select operations compared to MySQL. While insert performance was similar, PostgreSQL remained stable under concurrent select/insert scenarios, whereas MySQL degraded significantly [1].
*   **Write-Heavy Sysbench Tests**
    *   In write-heavy sysbench tests on a large server, MySQL (InnoDB) generally achieved higher average throughput in 6 out of 10 tests, with PostgreSQL outperforming in 3. PostgreSQL tended to write more I/O per operation and showed higher throughput variance. Notably, PostgreSQL showed 2.06x higher throughput for pure `insert` operations [3].
*   **Benchmarking Tools and Methodologies**
    *   One project provides a reproducible benchmark toolset for comparing relational database access layers in an Express.js service, covering native drivers and various access patterns like point reads, range scans, deep fetches, aggregations, and multi-statement transactions (including inserts and multi-row writes). This work emphasizes that performance is highly configuration-specific rather than a universal ranking [2].

### Features and Scalability for Write-Intensive Applications

Both databases are mature, ACID-compliant relational databases capable of handling large-scale, write-intensive workloads, with key differences in their feature sets and scaling ecosystems.

*   **When to Choose PostgreSQL**
    *   **Rich Features:** Offers a richer type system, more index options (partial, expression, GiST/GIN/BRIN), transactional DDL (allowing DDL rollbacks), full JSONB support, and extensive extensions (e.g., pgvector, PostGIS) [4, 5].
    *   **New Applications:** Often recommended as the default for new applications due to its comprehensive feature set and extensibility [4, 5].
    *   **Concurrency Model:** Uses a process-per-connection model and may require connection pooling (e.g., PgBouncer) for high concurrency [4, 5].
    *   **Sharding:** Scaling often involves custom application-layer sharding, logical sharding, Citus, PgBouncer, and read replicas [4, 6]. OpenAI and Figma are examples of companies successfully sharding PostgreSQL [6].
    *   **Memory/Restoration:** Uses the least idle memory and restores dumps significantly faster (5–8x faster in some tests) compared to MySQL/MariaDB [5].
*   **When to Choose MySQL (InnoDB)**
    *   **Operational Familiarity:** A strong choice if your team already has significant operational expertise with MySQL [4].
    *   **Simple Writes/PK Lookups:** Well-suited for workloads dominated by primary-key lookups and simple writes due to InnoDB’s clustered index and in-place updates [4].
    *   **Built-in Failover & Sharding:** Offers vendor-provided automatic failover (InnoDB Cluster) and robust sharding ecosystems like Vitess, which is heavily used by companies like Shopify and GitHub [4, 6].
    *   **DDL:** Each DDL statement is atomic with implicit commits, meaning DDL cannot be rolled back [4, 5].
    *   **Concurrency Model:** Uses a thread-per-connection model [4].
    *   **Replication:** Uses binary logs with GTIDs and Group Replication [4].
*   **MariaDB (Alternative to MySQL)**
    *   Similar to MySQL in behavior and use-cases, but with a smaller image, built-in vector search, and comparable write performance to PostgreSQL in some tests. It shares MySQL’s DDL drawback (no rollback) [5].

### Conclusion

For a write-heavy web application, the choice between PostgreSQL and MySQL depends heavily on specific workload characteristics, existing team expertise, and desired scaling architecture:

*   **PostgreSQL** appears to be a strong contender for applications requiring advanced data types, complex indexing, transactional DDL, and robust performance under concurrent read/write operations. While some pure write benchmarks show MySQL having an edge, PostgreSQL demonstrates superior select performance and stability in mixed workloads. Its rich feature set and extensibility make it a good default for new projects.
*   **MySQL (InnoDB)** excels in scenarios dominated by simple primary-key writes and benefits from a mature ecosystem for built-in failover and sharding (e.g., Vitess). If your team is already proficient in MySQL operations, its strengths for high-volume, straightforward writes can be leveraged.

Ultimately, both databases can scale to massive workloads. The most successful implementations rely on a well-designed architecture that leverages caching, replication, and appropriate sharding strategies, tailored to the specific database's strengths and tooling [6].

**Citations:**

1.  [MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-5903/16/10/382)

Essential results:

- PostgreSQL vs MySQL (InnoDB) are both mature, ACID-relational DBs suitable for web apps; choose based on architectural differences and ecosystem needs.
- When to pick PostgreSQL (default recommendation):
  - No constraints: PostgreSQL offers richer type system, more index options (partial, expression, GiST/GIN/BRIN), transactional DDL, full JSONB support, and extensive extensions.
  - You want built-in extensibility and advanced features in one database.
- When to pick MySQL (InnoDB):
  - Your team already operates MySQL well; operational competence matters.
  - Workload is dominated by primary-key lookups and simple writes; InnoDB’s clustered index and in-place updates suit high-volume PK workloads.
  - You want vendor-provided automatic failover (InnoDB Cluster) or you rely on Vitess sharding ecosystem.
- Replication and availability:
  - PostgreSQL: physical streaming replication (WAL) and logical replication; standby reads; hybrid upgrades across major versions possible with logical replication (but DDL not replicated in logical).
  - MySQL: binary log with GTIDs; Group Replication; built-in automatic failover.
- DDL and transactions:
  - PostgreSQL: most DDL is transactional and rollbacks are supported.
  - MySQL: each DDL statement is atomic with implicit commits.
- Sharding/Scaling paths:
  - PostgreSQL: Citus for sharding.
  - MySQL: Vitess for sharding.
- Other quick contrasts:
  - Connection model: PostgreSQL uses a process per connection; MySQL uses a thread per connection.
  - Storage: PostgreSQL stores rows in a heap with pointers from all indexes; MySQL uses a clustered B-tree on primary key with secondary indexes pointing to keys.
  - Isolation default: PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED; MySQL REPEATABLE READ.
  - Materialized views: PostgreSQL yes; MySQL no.

Bottom line guidance:
- If starting fresh: PostgreSQL is often the better all-in-one choice due to DDL transactional support, richer data types, and broader index/extension options.
- If you already run MySQL well or need built-in failover and easy sharding with Vitess, MySQL/InnoDB is compelling.

Bottom line guidance:
- Choose PostgreSQL for new apps needing advanced features, best dump/restore performance, and lower idle memory.
- Choose MySQL for PHP-focused apps needing fast reads and straightforward tooling, accepting potential write-speed cost from binary logging and limited rollback for DDL.
- Choose MariaDB for similar use-cases as MySQL but with a smaller image, built-in vector/search features, and comparable write performance to PostgreSQL.

Summary:
- This work presents a reproducible benchmark toolset and experimental design for comparing relational database access layers in an Express.js service, specifically PostgreSQL vs. MySQL, across multiple engines, configurations, and workloads.
- The benchmark covers native drivers and access patterns such as point reads, keyset range scans, deep/nested fetches, aggregations, and multi-statement transactions (including inserts and multi-row writes). It measures throughput (requests per second) and tail latency (p50, p90, p97.5, p99) under controlled conditions.
- Over revisions (v1.2 to v1.4), the study introduces rigorous statistical analysis (paired tests, Wilcoxon, TOST, paired p-values), CPU/resource accounting, and multiple targeted experiments:
  - Connection-pool size sensitivity
  - Single-host resource isolation
  - Transactional multi-statement write workloads
  - Multi-worker (node cluster) setups showing native drivers overtaking ORM layers when cores are fully utilized
  - Per-layer pool-size frontiers and mixed read/write workloads
  - Longer-run sensitivity checks and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all throughput results
  - Open-loop and closed-loop tail analyses with controlled utilization to examine saturated tails
- The findings emphasize configuration-specific performance determinants rather than a universal ranking. Key takeaways include:
  - Under matched utilization and tested configurations, native drivers may outperform ORM layers in certain patterns, especially when CPU cores are fully utilized.
  - The saturated tail (p99) is heavily influenced by workload mix, concurrency, and resource isolation; tail behavior stabilizes under matched utilization in some experiments but can diverge under others depending on the layer and workload.
  - The deep-fetch performance characteristics are consistent in relative terms across experiments, but the absolute growth pattern was clarified to be a roughly fixed multiplier with respect to graph size rather than a continuously growing factor.
- The work provides a replication package with the benchmark harness, paper sources, results, and an online supplement (Tables S1–S26) for detailed methodology, control settings, and statistical analyses.

Summary:
- Both PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) are mature, ACID-relational databases suitable for web apps; the choice depends on architectural differences and project constraints.
- When to choose PostgreSQL (default recommendation):
  - No constraints: PostgreSQL offers richer types, broader index options (including partial and expression indexes), transactional DDL, JSONB, and useful extensions, reducing the need for multiple systems.
- When to choose MySQL (InnoDB) (or keep if already in use):
  - Your team is already proficient with MySQL.
  - Workloads dominated by primary-key lookups and simple writes, benefiting from InnoDB’s clustered primary-key index and in-place updates.
  - You want built-in automatic failover (Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster) without extra tooling.
  - You plan to shard via ecosystems like Vitess (MySQL) or similar tools.
- Key architectural differences (highlights):
  - Storage and indexing: PostgreSQL uses heap storage with indexes pointing to row locations; MySQL/InnoDB uses a clustered B+tree on the primary key plus secondary indexes that reference the PK.
  - Old row versions: PostgreSQL keeps old versions in the table with VACUUM cleanup; MySQL uses undo logs and purge threads.
  - Isolation: PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED; MySQL defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
  - DDL: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL; MySQL’s DDL is atomic per statement but commits are implicit.
  - Replication and failover: PostgreSQL offers physical streaming and logical replication; MySQL offers binary log replication with Group Replication and InnoDB Cluster for automatic failover.
  - Extensions and ecosystem: PostgreSQL emphasizes extensions (types, indexes, languages); MySQL relies on plugins and pluggable storage engines.
  - Licensing: PostgreSQL uses a permissive PostgreSQL license; MySQL Community uses GPLv2 with commercial licenses available.

What this means for decision:
- If you’re starting fresh with no constraints, PostgreSQL is generally the more capable “one database” choice.
- If you’re already well-versed in MySQL, or need built-in failover and easy sharding paths, MySQL may be preferable.
- For sharding, consider Vitess (MySQL) vs. Citus (PostgreSQL). Keep isolation levels deliberate and plan for connection pooling and short transactions.

Summary:

- MySQL (InnoDB)
  - Storage: Clustered index (B+Tree); table data stored in leaf nodes; secondary indexes point to primary key.
  - Updates: In-place updates using Undo Log for MVCC; if updated data doesn’t grow, writes overwrite in place. Only necessary data changes; unchanged indexes remain intact.
  - Deletes: Marked as deleted with a delete flag at leaf; freed space reused from a free list when new inserts fit the gap.
  - Best for: Write-heavy workloads with frequent in-place updates; stable I/O with predictable latency.

- PostgreSQL
  - Storage: Heap storage; data stored in a heap with indexes (including primary/secondary) as private B-Tree structures containing CTIDs (pointers to heap tuples).
  - Updates: Logical delete + insert of a new row; never overwrites old data to preserve MVCC integrity.
  - Deletes: Old rows become dead tuples; VACUUM must reclaim space. Can lead to table bloat if autovacuum is not well-tuned.
  - Best for: Read-heavy, analytic workloads, complex data types, and scenarios where MVCC integrity and data versioning are critical.

Bottom line:
- If you need heavy in-place updates with stable I/O and a finite set of records updated frequently, MySQL/InnoDB is preferable.
- If you prioritize MVCC integrity, complex queries, and can tolerate write amplification and periodic vacuuming, PostgreSQL is stronger.

runs.report:
## PostgreSQL vs. MySQL for Write-Heavy Web Applications

This report compares PostgreSQL and MySQL, focusing on their performance and suitability for write-heavy web applications, based on recent benchmarks and architectural analyses.

### Performance Benchmarks

Recent benchmarks generally indicate PostgreSQL's strong performance in write-heavy scenarios, though specific workload characteristics can influence results.

*   **Overall Throughput and Latency**
    *   PostgreSQL generally shows significantly higher throughput (QPS) and consistently lower latency across mixed and write-heavy workloads compared to MySQL. One benchmark shows PostgreSQL with ~3.7x higher throughput on mixed workloads [source](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
    *   PostgreSQL 17 outperforms MySQL 8.4 in 5 out of 6 transactional SaaS workloads in 2026, demonstrating better write throughput [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).

*   **Specific Write Operations**
    *   **Inserts:** PostgreSQL shows marked improvements, with up to ~4.87x throughput gain and 3.5–11x faster latency for single-row inserts [source](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html). Another test showed PostgreSQL +14% for single-row inserts [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   **Updates:** PostgreSQL demonstrates a ~4.2–4.82x throughput advantage and ~6–10x faster latency for multi-column updates [source](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html). Single-row updates were +19% for PostgreSQL [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   **Deletes:** PostgreSQL exhibits a ~3.3–4.65x throughput advantage and ~9–10x faster latency [source](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html). PostgreSQL was +17% for single-row deletes [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   **Batch Inserts:** MySQL 8.4 can be competitive or slightly better for batch inserts (e.g., +2.5% for 100-row batch inserts) due to InnoDB's change buffer [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   **JSON Writes:** PostgreSQL's JSONB type shows superior write performance, with +24% throughput over MySQL's JSON [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).
    *   **Update-Index & Update-Zipf:** Some specific write-heavy scenarios (e.g., update-index and update-zipf with no caching and long runs) show InnoDB with ~1.09x to 1.55x higher throughput on average, though PostgreSQL often performs more write I/O per operation and InnoDB uses more CPU [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).

*   **Other Performance Considerations**
    *   **Stability:** InnoDB (MySQL) tends to show more stable throughput with less variance across tests compared to PostgreSQL, which can exhibit high variability [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).
    *   **IO and CPU Usage:** PostgreSQL often performs more write I/O per operation in several tests, while InnoDB typically uses more CPU and context switches [source](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2026/06/write-heavy-sysbench-tests-large-server.html).
    *   **Binary Log Impact:** MySQL's binary log (on by default) can impact write throughput; disabling it improves some benchmarks but sacrifices point-in-time recovery [source](https://www.melonslab.com/guides/postgresql-vs-mysql-vs-mariadb).

### Architectural Differences for Write Operations

The fundamental differences in how PostgreSQL and MySQL handle data storage and updates significantly impact their performance in write-heavy environments.

*   **Data Storage and Indexing**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Uses heap storage where data is stored in a heap, and indexes (primary/secondary) are B-tree structures containing CTIDs (pointers to heap tuples) [source](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf), [source](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   **MySQL (InnoDB):** Uses a clustered index (B+Tree) where table data is stored in the leaf nodes of the primary key index. Secondary indexes point to the primary key [source](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf), [source](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).

*   **Updates and Deletes**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Handles updates as a logical delete of the old row and an insert of a new row, never overwriting old data to maintain MVCC integrity. Deleted rows become "dead tuples" that require VACUUM to reclaim space, potentially leading to table bloat if not properly tuned [source](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf).
    *   **MySQL (InnoDB):** Performs in-place updates using an Undo Log for MVCC. If updated data doesn't grow, writes overwrite in place. Deleted rows are marked with a flag, and their space is reused from a free list when new inserts fit the gap [source](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf). This design can be better for write-heavy workloads with frequent in-place updates, offering more stable I/O and predictable latency [source](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf).

*   **Transaction Handling & MVCC**
    *   **PostgreSQL:** Defaults to READ COMMITTED isolation. Its MVCC implementation keeps old row versions within the table, relying on VACUUM for cleanup [source](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter). Supports transactional DDL [source](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).
    *   **MySQL (InnoDB):** Defaults to REPEATABLE READ isolation. Uses undo logs and purge threads for old row versions. DDL is atomic per statement, with implicit commits [source](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter).

### Recommendations for Write-Heavy Web Applications

*   **PostgreSQL is generally recommended for new write-heavy web applications**, especially those with transactional SaaS workloads, JSON-heavy data, multi-tenant architectures, or a need for advanced features and extensibility [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks), [source](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter). Its consistent higher throughput and lower latency across most write operations make it a strong contender [source](https://binaryigor.com/mysql-vs-postgresql-performance.html).
*   **Consider MySQL (InnoDB) if:**
    *   Your team is already proficient with MySQL, and the application's write patterns are dominated by primary-key lookups and simple, in-place updates benefiting from InnoDB's clustered index [source](https://dpkdb.com/article/postgresql-vs-mysql-the-differences-that-matter), [source](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf).
    *   The application heavily relies on batch inserts, where MySQL can be competitive or slightly outperform PostgreSQL [source](https://johal.in/postgres-17-vs-mysql-84-write-throughput-benchmarks).

Be aware of PostgreSQL's VACUUM requirements to prevent table bloat [source](https://dev.to/quangpv/how-the-two-most-popular-open-source-databases-mysql-postgresql-handle-insert-update-delete-4klf).

Summary:
- Both PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) are mature, ACID-relational databases suitable for web apps; the choice depends on architectural differences and project constraints.
- When to choose PostgreSQL (default recommendation):
  - No constraints: PostgreSQL offers richer types, broader index options (including partial and expression indexes), transactional DDL, JSONB, and useful extensions, reducing the need for multiple systems.
- When to choose MySQL (InnoDB) (or keep if already in use):
  - Your team is already proficient with MySQL.
  - Workloads dominated by primary-key lookups and simple writes, benefiting from InnoDB’s clustered primary-key index and in-place updates.
  - You want built-in automatic failover (Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster) without extra tooling.
  - You plan to shard via ecosystems like Vitess (MySQL) or similar tools.
- Key architectural differences (highlights):
  - Storage and indexing: PostgreSQL uses heap storage with indexes pointing to row locations; MySQL/InnoDB uses a clustered B+tree on the primary key plus secondary indexes that reference the PK.
  - Old row versions: PostgreSQL keeps old versions in the table with VACUUM cleanup; MySQL uses undo logs and purge threads.
  - Isolation: PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED; MySQL defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
  - DDL: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL; MySQL’s DDL is atomic per statement but commits are implicit.
  - Replication and failover: PostgreSQL offers physical streaming and logical replication; MySQL offers binary log replication with Group Replication and InnoDB Cluster for automatic failover.
  - Extensions and ecosystem: PostgreSQL emphasizes extensions (types, indexes, languages); MySQL relies on plugins and pluggable storage engines.
  - Licensing: PostgreSQL uses a permissive PostgreSQL license; MySQL Community uses GPLv2 with commercial licenses available.

What this means for decision:
- If you’re starting fresh with no constraints, PostgreSQL is generally the more capable “one database” choice.
- If you’re already well-versed in MySQL, or need built-in failover and easy sharding paths, MySQL may be preferable.
- For sharding, consider Vitess (MySQL) vs. Citus (PostgreSQL). Keep isolation levels deliberate and plan for connection pooling and short transactions.

Summary:

- Scope: Write-heavy sysbench tests on a large server comparing modern Postgres (16.13, 17.9, 18.3, 19 beta1) vs. MySQL 8.4.7 with InnoDB. Tests are long (2 hours each), with large tables not fitting in memory, and include post-test vacuum. Aimed to detect MVCC/GC-related overhead and potential regressions.

Key results:
- Throughput (relative to Postgres 15.17 baseline):
  - InnoDB generally offers higher average throughput than Postgres in 6 of 10 tests, similar in 1 test, and lower in 3 tests.
  - Postgres 16–19 show throughput variation and potential regression signals in some tests.
- Update-index and update-zipf:
  - InnoDB outperforms Postgres by about 1.55x (update-index) and ~1.09x (update-zipf) on average.
  - Per-operation write I/O is higher for Postgres; InnoDB uses more CPU and more context switches.
  - Autovacuum likely running; manual vacuum occurs after tests.
- Insert tests:
  - Postgres outperforms InnoDB by about 2.06x on average.
  - Per-operation write I/O is higher for Postgres; Postgres also uses more CPU and context switches.
- IO characteristics (iostat/vmstat, normalized by operation rate):
  - Postgres 19b1 shows high write IO and activity; MySQL shows different but substantial IO/CPU patterns.
  - CPU and context-switch behavior differ between engines depending on test type.

Bottom line:
- Postgres throughput appears more variable and may show regressions across newer versions for certain write-heavy patterns.
- InnoDB generally achieves higher throughput in most tests except insert-heavy workloads where Postgres leads.
- Per-operation storage I/O trends differ: Postgres tends to write more per operation in several tests; InnoDB often uses more CPU and context switches.
- Overall, MySQL/InnoDB offers better throughput in the majority of non-insert workloads, while Postgres can dominate in inserts.

results.search_result:
Essential results from the benchmark (MySQL vs Postgres, with 17rc1/15.8 and 8.0.39/5.6.51):

- Postgres 17rc1 vs 15.8
  - Writes: mostly similar; minor improvements in some write-heavy steps.
  - Reads: largely unchanged; small gains in some read-heavy steps.

- MySQL 8.0.39 vs 5.6.51
  - Writes: significantly faster (roughly 2.5x to 4x faster).
  - Reads: mixed to slower (read-heavy steps 12–27% slower).

- MySQL vs Postgres (overall)
  - Point queries: MySQL 8.0.39 faster (roughly comparable QPS to Postgres on point queries); MySQL accesses PK index only (InnoDB) vs Postgres accessing PK then heap.
  - Writes and range queries: Postgres 17rc1 faster on write-heavy and range queries.
  - In less IO-bound scenarios (smaller datasets fitting in cache): Postgres tends to outperform on writes/range; MySQL excels on point queries.
  - In more IO-bound scenarios (larger datasets, more IO): Postgres generally retains an edge on writes/range queries; MySQL improves substantially on writes but can incur more IO for reads.

- Specific context by workload
  - Cached workload: improvements for Postgres writes in 17rc1; MySQL shows strong write gains for 8.0.39 vs 5.6.51.
  - Less IO-bound (64M rows per table): Postgres leads on write-heavy and range; MySQL dominates on point queries.
  - More IO-bound (200M rows per table): similar trend; Postgres faster for writes/range; MySQL faster on point queries but overall IO costs higher for reads in some cases.

Bottom line: If your priority is point queries, MySQL 8.0.39 is faster. If you care about writes or range queries, Postgres 17rc1 generally leads, especially in write-heavy or IO-bound scenarios. MySQL shows large gains over older 5.6.51 in writes, with mixed read performance.
