## CRISPR Base Editing vs. Prime Editing: A Comparative Report

This report summarizes the key differences, capabilities, limitations, and therapeutic potential of CRISPR base editing and prime editing, two advanced gene-editing technologies.

### Mechanisms and Core Capabilities

*   **Base Editing (BE)**
    *   **Mechanism:** Base editors facilitate precise single-nucleotide changes (e.g., C-to-T, A-to-G) without creating a double-strand break (DSB) in the DNA. They achieve this by fusing a Cas protein (often a Cas9 nickase) with a nucleobase deaminase [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9), https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes).
    *   **Edit Types:** Primarily enables all 4 transition mutations (C-to-T, G-to-A, A-to-G, T-to-C) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
    *   **Advantages:** Works in both dividing and non-dividing cells, offering broader tissue targeting than methods relying on homology-directed repair (HDR) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
    *   **Limitations:** Can cause genome-wide or off-target mutations via the deaminase, bystander effects, and broad editing windows https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes), [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3).

*   **Prime Editing (PE)**
    *   **Mechanism:** Prime editing is a "search-and-replace" method that fuses a Cas9 nickase with an engineered reverse transcriptase, guided by a pegRNA (prime editing guide RNA) that specifies the target and encodes the desired edit [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9), https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes), https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9). It operates without creating DSBs or requiring donor DNA templates [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9), https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9).
    *   **Edit Types:** Enables all 12 possible base-to-base conversions, as well as small insertions and deletions (indels) https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes), https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9). This expands the range of correctable mutations beyond common transition mutations [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
    *   **Advantages:** Offers high versatility and can correct a broader range of mutation types compared to base editors [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/), https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes).
    *   **Limitations:** Editing efficiency is relatively low and highly variable across targets, cell types, and conditions (often below 20% in immortalized cell lines, even lower in primary cells) https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9). The large size of the PE construct complicates delivery, especially for AAV-based *in vivo* applications https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9). It also requires careful design of PBS length, RT template, edit location, and gRNA choice https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes).

### Therapeutic Potential and Applications

*   **Shared Therapeutic Promise**
    *   Both base editing and prime editing show strong therapeutic potential for correcting a large share of pathogenic human SNPs, with estimates suggesting possible correction of up to ~89% of known pathogenic variants in ClinVar [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
    *   They are promising for autosomal dominant conditions and diseases with large or hard-to-deliver genes [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
    *   Early demonstrations have corrected pathogenic mutations in animal models, human cell lines, and human zygotes [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).

*   **Distinct Applications**
    *   **Base Editing:** Particularly suited for single-base changes, such as correcting common transition mutations [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
    *   **Prime Editing:** Highly versatile for precise base substitutions, small insertions, and deletions, making it promising for polygenic diseases and complex variants https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9).

### Challenges and Future Directions

*   **Delivery:** Safe and effective delivery of both base editors and prime editors to specific tissues in humans remains a major hurdle to clinical translation [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/). Tissue-targeting challenges and deliverability beyond the liver are current bottlenecks [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3).
*   **Off-target Effects:** While both methods aim to reduce DSBs, base editors can still cause off-target activity, and prime editing also faces potential off-target concerns https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes), [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3).
*   **Efficiency:** Prime editing generally has lower and more variable editing efficiency https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9).
*   **Safety and Long-term Effects:** Clinical translation is in early stages, requiring careful monitoring of long-term safety and risks, including potential DNA damage accumulation and rare oncogenic events, although no therapy-editing-related tumors have been reported in trials to date [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3).
*   **Ongoing Refinements:**
    *   Efforts are focused on improving efficiency, targeting scope, and product purity for both technologies [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
    *   For prime editing, strategies include engineering improved PE proteins, optimizing pegRNA design, modulating mismatch repair pathways, and refining delivery methods https://www.cell.com/biotechnology/fulltext/S0167-7799(23)00085-9 (unverified)00085-9).
    *   Interdisciplinary advances like synthetic biology and AI-driven design are expected to improve target identification, outcome prediction, and editing efficiency [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12967-024-05957-3).

### Conclusion

Base editing and prime editing represent powerful, versatile CRISPR-based tools for precise genome modification without inducing double-strand breaks. While base editors are excellent for specific single-base changes, prime editors offer broader versatility for various edit types including small insertions and deletions. Both technologies hold significant therapeutic promise but require continued advancements in delivery, efficiency, specificity, and *in vivo* validation before widespread clinical use.

Summary:
- DNA base-editing and prime-editing are CRISPR-based methods that install precise nucleotide changes without creating double-strand breaks, enabling targeted point mutations in cellular DNA.
- Therapeutic potential is high: over 25% of pathogenic human SNPs can be corrected with four transition mutations; prime-editing could, in principle, correct up to ~89% of known disease-associated variants in ClinVar.
- These editors work in both dividing and non-dividing (terminally differentiated) cells, unlike HDR-based CRISPR approaches restricted to S/G2 phases, broadening applicability for gene therapy.
- Base-editing advantages include feasibility for large genes (delivery constraints with viral vectors) and suitability for autosomal dominant diseases where silencing/ablation is not viable.
- Developments include CRISPR-Pass and various improvements that expand targeting scope and editing purity; initial work has demonstrated corrections in animal models, human cell lines, and even human tripronuclear zygotes.
- Practical challenges remain, the most critical being safe and efficient delivery to specific tissues in humans. Ongoing work aims to enhance efficiency, targeting scope, and edit quality to realize clinical potential.

In short, base-editing and prime-editing offer precise, potentially therapeutic nucleotide corrections across a broad range of genetic diseases, with substantial progress shown in models, but delivery to human tissues remains the principal hurdle.

- CRISPRa/i offers reversible, non-permanent control of gene expression and can address conditions where altering expression is therapeutic. Examples include lipid-nanoparticle–delivered epigenetic editors that markedly reduce PCSK9 and LDL cholesterol in animals.
- CAR-T therapies using CRISPR editing extend beyond cancer to autoimmune diseases. An allogeneic, multiplex-edited CAR-T product showed inflammation reversal and functional improvement in myositis and systemic sclerosis without major adverse events, though multiplex editing carries risks (e.g., large deletions, translocations). This has spurred interest in safer approaches like base/prime editors.
- Long-term safety remains a key concern due to limited follow-up on some therapies; ex vivo approaches show partial safety signals but more data are needed.
- Overall, CRISPR’s therapeutic potential hinges on overcoming delivery, specificity, persistence, scalability, and regulatory challenges. AI-driven advances are expected to accelerate nuclease engineering, design safer/editing components, and optimize delivery platforms, shaping precision medicine in the next decade.

# CRISPR Base Editing vs. Prime Editing: A Comparative Report

## Overview of CRISPR-based Genome Editing

CRISPR-based genome editing tools offer precise methods for altering DNA sequences. While traditional CRISPR-Cas nucleases create double-strand breaks (DSBs) to enable edits via cellular repair, base editors and prime editors represent advanced approaches that aim to achieve precise nucleotide changes without inducing DSBs. This distinction is crucial for reducing unintended mutations (indels) and expanding therapeutic applicability [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/), [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).

## Base Editing

Base editing is a CRISPR-based method designed to introduce precise single-base changes (transition mutations) without creating DSBs [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).

### Mechanism and Capabilities
*   **Targeted Point Mutations**: Base editors fuse CRISPR/Cas with nucleobase deaminases to enable single-base substitutions https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes).
*   **Types of Edits**:
    *   Cytosine base editors (CBEs) convert C to T.
    *   Adenine base editors (ABEs) convert A to G.
    *   Glycosylase base editors (GBEs) convert C to G.
    *   Dual-base editors (DBEs) can perform simultaneous C to T and A to G edits https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7 (unverified)00325-7).
*   **DSB-Free**: A key advantage is the avoidance of double-strand breaks, which can lead to undesirable insertions or deletions (indels) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).

### Applications and Limitations
*   **Therapeutic Potential**: Base editing is suitable for correcting over 25% of pathogenic human single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that can be addressed by the four transition mutations it facilitates [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/). It is also feasible for large genes and autosomal dominant diseases where silencing/ablation isn't an option [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
*   **Off-target Concerns**: Off-target effects are a notable consideration, primarily driven by the deaminase activity and gRNA/Cas targeting https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes).
*   **Limited Scope**: While precise, base editors cannot realize all types of base substitutions or certain insertions/deletions [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).

## Prime Editing

Prime editing is a more versatile CRISPR-based "search-and-replace" approach that allows for a broader range of precise genomic alterations without creating DSBs or requiring donor DNA templates [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).

### Mechanism and Capabilities
*   **Combined System**: Prime editors combine a Cas9 nickase with a reverse transcriptase, guided by a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z), https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7 (unverified)00325-7).
*   **Versatile Edits**: Prime editing can introduce all base substitutions, as well as targeted small insertions and deletions (indels) [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9), https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7 (unverified)00325-7). This overcomes limitations of base editors which are restricted to certain base transitions [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).
*   **DSB-Free**: Like base editing, prime editing also operates without inducing double-strand breaks [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).

### Applications and Limitations
*   **Broad Therapeutic Scope**: Prime editing could, in principle, correct up to approximately 89% of known disease-associated variants in ClinVar [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/).
*   **Design Complexity**: Requires careful design considerations, including PBS length, RT template, edit location, and gRNA selection https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes).
*   **Efficiency and Off-target Profiling**: Early prime editing systems (PE1) showed limited efficiency (0.7%–5.5% for edits) and incomplete genome-wide off-target profiling https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7 (unverified)00325-7), https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes (unverified)30150-X?rss=yes).

## Key Differences and Considerations

| Feature               | Base Editing                                                                  | Prime Editing                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| :-------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Edit Type**         | Specific single-base transitions (C to T, A to G, C to G)                     | All 12 types of base-to-base substitutions, small insertions, and small deletions                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Mechanism**         | Cas-deaminase fusion                                                          | Cas9 nickase-reverse transcriptase fusion guided by pegRNA                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **DSB Formation**     | No                                                                            | No                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Donor DNA**         | Not required                                                                  | Not required                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Versatility**       | Limited to specific transition mutations                                      | Highly versatile; enables a broad range of precise edits, overcoming limitations of base editing                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Therapeutic Scope** | Can correct ~25% of pathogenic SNPs via transition mutations                  | Can, in principle, correct ~89% of known disease-associated variants                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Complexity**        | Relatively simpler design                                                     | More complex design involving pegRNA, PBS length, and RT template                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Off-target Effects**| Primarily driven by deaminase activity; active research on mitigation strategies | Requires careful design, with ongoing work to fully profile genome-wide off-target effects                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

## Current Challenges and Future Directions

Both base editing and prime editing offer significant advantages over traditional CRISPR methods by avoiding DSBs and enabling precise edits [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/). However, substantial challenges remain, particularly in safe and efficient delivery to specific human tissues, especially for large genes or editors that exceed viral vector (AAV) cargo capacity [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/), https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7 (unverified)00325-7). Ongoing research focuses on enhancing efficiency, expanding targeting scope, improving edit quality, and refining delivery platforms to realize their full clinical potential in gene therapy [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7503568/), https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-medicine/fulltext/S2666-3791(25)00532-4 (unverified)00532-4). There is no "one-size-fits-all" editor; the choice depends on the desired edit type, target site constraints, delivery method, and acceptable risk of off-target activity [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).

Summary:
- DNA base-editing and prime-editing are CRISPR-based methods that install precise nucleotide changes without creating double-strand breaks, enabling targeted point mutations in cellular DNA.
- Therapeutic potential is high: over 25% of pathogenic human SNPs can be corrected with four transition mutations; prime-editing could, in principle, correct up to ~89% of known disease-associated variants in ClinVar.
- These editors work in both dividing and non-dividing (terminally differentiated) cells, unlike HDR-based CRISPR approaches restricted to S/G2 phases, broadening applicability for gene therapy.
- Base-editing advantages include feasibility for large genes (delivery constraints with viral vectors) and suitability for autosomal dominant diseases where silencing/ablation is not viable.
- Developments include CRISPR-Pass and various improvements that expand targeting scope and editing purity; initial work has demonstrated corrections in animal models, human cell lines, and even human tripronuclear zygotes.
- Practical challenges remain, the most critical being safe and efficient delivery to specific tissues in humans. Ongoing work aims to enhance efficiency, targeting scope, and edit quality to realize clinical potential.

In short, base-editing and prime-editing offer precise, potentially therapeutic nucleotide corrections across a broad range of genetic diseases, with substantial progress shown in models, but delivery to human tissues remains the principal hurdle.

Summary of essential results

- Scope and purpose: This review surveys the four main classes of CRISPR–Cas genome editing tools—nucleases, base editors, transposases/recombinases, and prime editors—and discusses their capabilities, limitations, targeting scope, and editing specificity. It emphasizes practical guidance for selecting tools for basic research and therapeutic applications.

- Tool classes and capabilities:
  - CRISPR–Cas nucleases: Traditional programmable DNA endonucleases that create double-strand breaks to enable edits via cellular repair pathways; offers broad targeting but requires careful control of on-target/off-target effects.
  - Base editors: Enable precise single-base changes (transition mutations) without creating double-strand breaks; expand the ability to install point mutations with potentially reduced indel formation.
  - Transposases/recombinases: Integrate or rearrange DNA using transposon or recombination systems, enabling targeted insertions or excisions in certain contexts; expanding the repertoire beyond nuclease-induced breaks.
  - Prime editors: Combine Cas with reverse transcriptase to introduce targeted base substitutions, small insertions, and deletions without double-strand breaks or donor DNA templates; offers versatile editing with high precision.

- Design and decision guidance:
  - The article provides decision trees and figures to help researchers choose among base editors and other tools based on desired edit type, PAM compatibility, editing window, and acceptable trade-offs between efficiency and specificity.
  - It discusses strategies to improve specificity and minimize off-target effects, as well as considerations for delivery, cell type, and experimental context.

- Emerging technologies and future directions:
  - Highlights ongoing development of transposase-based and prime editor approaches to broaden targeting scope, improve editing outcomes, and enable therapeutic applications.
  - Points to opportunities for combining tools and developing new variants to address challenging edits, expand PAM compatibility, and further refine safety profiles.

- Therapeutic and research impact:
  - The review underscores the rapid translation of several CRISPR-derived tools into preclinical and clinical settings, while acknowledging regulatory and safety considerations, including potential off-target effects and immunogenicity.

- Overall takeaway:
  - There is no one-size-fits-all editor; the choice depends on the desired edit type (point mutation, insertion/deletion, large integration), target site constraints (PAM, editing window), delivery method, and acceptable risk of off-target activity. Continuous improvements in precision, scope, and delivery are driving broader applications in basic research and therapeutics.

Prime editing is presented as a transformative, versatile genome-editing approach that expands beyond the limitations of CRISPR-based double-strand break (DSB) methods and base editing. Key points:

- Concept: Prime editing uses a programmable reverse-transcriptase fused to a Cas9 nickase guided by a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) to search for and replace genomic sequences without requiring DSBs or donor DNA.
- Versatility: Supports a wide range of precise edits, including all base substitutions, targeted insertions and deletions, and combinations thereof—addressing many types of genomic modifications that were difficult or impossible with previous methods.
- Limitations of prior methods:
  - Traditional CRISPR/Cas9 with homology-directed repair relies on DSBs, often causing indels and low precision.
  - Base editors enable some base transitions (e.g., C-to-T, A-to-G) without DSBs but cannot realize all substitutions or certain insertions/deletions.
- Impact: By enabling a “search-and-replace” mechanism, prime editing overcomes these limitations, broadening the scope of precise in situ genomic alterations.
- Original foundational work: Anzalone et al., Nature 2019, described the initial prime editing system (search-and-replace without DSBs or donor DNA).
- Context: The article frames prime editing as redefining precision genome editing, highlighting its potential to advance functional genomics and therapeutic strategies while acknowledging ongoing optimization for efficiency, specificity, and delivery.

results.search_result:
Summary:
- Mercury is a naturally occurring, toxic element found in air, water, and soil; exposure can cause serious health problems, especially harming fetal development.
- Health effects span the nervous, digestive, immune systems, lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes, with notable risks to unborn children from methylmercury exposure.
- Humans are exposed mainly via inhalation of mercury vapor (industrial settings) and consumption of methylmercury in fish and shellfish. Ethylmercury (in thiomersal) found in some vaccines is not considered a health risk.
- Mercury is one of WHO’s top ten chemicals of major public health concern.
- Key action priorities: eliminate mercury mining and reduce use in gold mining; promote mercury-free and safer alternatives; prevent exposure from heritage uses (thermometers, measuring devices); manage mercury in products (batteries, lamps, dental amalgam, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals).
- Coal burning is a major source of atmospheric mercury emissions.
- Inorganic mercury salts are corrosive and can cause kidney and other toxic effects; various forms (elemental, inorganic, organic) have different toxic profiles.

If you want, I can tailor this to a specific aspect (health effects, exposure sources, or policy actions).
results.title: Mercury

results.query: health effects of mercury exposure to humans
results.search_result:
Summary:

- Mercury effects span three chemical forms: elemental mercury, inorganic mercury salts, and methylmercury (implied under “three chemical categories”).
- Across all forms, the most consistently observed health impacts are neurological and renal effects in humans and animals.

Elemental mercury (vapor exposure):
- Neurological: tremor, vision and motor coordination impairment, cognitive deficits (memory, integrated function), mood/behavioral symptoms (mood swings, irritability, nervousness, timidity).
- Renal: reduced glomerular function and tubular injury reported epidemiologically; dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity in animals.
- Other: at high/fatal exposure, respiratory toxicity (pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, respiratory failure) observed; no strong evidence for other organ targets in broad studies.

Inorganic mercury salts:
- Neurological and renal toxicity consistently observed in animal studies (oral exposure).
- Other potential effects suggested in animals: cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive; some carcinogenic signals in male rats (forestomach, thyroid).
- No human epidemiology studies identified for inorganic mercury salts specifically.

Methylmercury (implied under inorganic/other categories):
- Neurological: developmental neurotoxicity (hyperactivity, impaired motor coordination, memory, sociability); adult neurobehavioral effects (hyperactivity, impaired learning/memory) and overt neurotoxic signs in animals.
- Renal: nephrotoxicity with dose- and duration-dependent severity.
- Cardiovascular: some evidence of blood pressure changes and altered cardiac function.
- Immunological/Reproductive: potential immune stimulation and reduced fertility markers in susceptible animals.
- Cancer: limited evidence of carcinogenicity in male rats (forestomach, thyroid).

Epidemiological context:
- For elemental mercury: consistent neurological effects in exposed adults; some renal decrements.
- For methylmercury: data largely from fish/high fish diet exposures; cardiovascular and other systemic associations exist but are less consistently characterized across all populations.

Overall takeaway:
- Neurological and renal toxicity are the most consistently observed health effects across mercury forms, with additional potential cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive, and carcinogenic findings mostly from animal studies or specific exposure contexts.

results.search_result:
Summary:
- Mercury is a neurotoxin whose health effects depend on form (methylmercury vs. metallic/inorganic), dose, duration, exposure route, age (unborn infants most vulnerable), and individual health.
- Methylmercury exposure mainly from eating fish/shellfish with high levels; most people have low blood levels but high exposure can harm the brain and nervous system, especially in fetuses and young children. Possible symptoms: visual field loss, tingling, poor coordination, speech/hearing/walking impairments, muscle weakness; prenatal exposure can affect brain development and cognitive/motor skills.
- Metallic mercury exposure occurs mainly via inhalation of vapor (from spills/products). Acute/prolonged exposure can cause tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular issues, headaches, sensory disturbances, and impaired mental function; high exposure may damage kidneys, respiratory system, and cause death.
- Inorganic mercury exposure can damage the gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, and kidneys; symptoms include skin issues, mood/memory disturbances, mental changes, and muscle weakness.
- If concerned about mercury exposure, consult a physician or poison control (1-800-222-1222). Some EPA drinking water MCLs exist for inorganic mercury to limit exposure.

results.search_result:
Essential results from EPA’s How People are Exposed to Mercury:

- Primary exposure: Most Americans are exposed to methylmercury mainly by eating fish and shellfish that contain it. Most people have trace amounts in their bodies, typically below levels of health concern.
- How methylmercury forms and accumulates: Mercury enters air from various sources, settles into water/land, and microorganisms convert it to methylmercury, which builds up in fish. Levels are higher in larger, longer-lived, predator fish.
- Exposure details: Other exposures come from using or breaking products that contain mercury. Inhalation of mercury vapor from broken containers or devices can be dangerous, especially in poorly ventilated indoor spaces. Accidental ingestion of metallic mercury is possible but generally lower risk than inhalation.
- Specific scenarios: Common household items (thermometers, certain jewelry pendants) can release mercury if broken; rapid cleanup and proper handling are advised. High-level, prolonged vapor exposure can cause serious health effects.
- Health guidance: If concerned about exposure, contact a health care provider. Learn and follow proper cleanup steps for mercury spills (thermometers, broken devices) and be aware of products that historically contained mercury.
- Broader context: Mercury compounds have been used in various products (fungicides, preservatives, antiseptics) but many uses have been discontinued. Some products are still encountered, including those manufactured abroad or sold illicitly.

Summary:

- Main risk: Methylmercury (MeHg) mainly harms the nervous system, with particular concern for embryo neurodevelopment and young children due to MeHg crossing the placenta and blood-brain barriers.
- Exposure and risk: Across all scenarios, combined exposure from food, water, soil, and air remains below EFSA weekly tolerable intakes (TWIs) for both MeHg (1.3 µg/kg bw) and inorganic mercury (4 µg/kg bw). ## Is Mercury Safe?

Mercury is a naturally occurring, toxic element that poses serious health risks, particularly to the nervous system and developing fetuses. Its safety is dependent on its chemical form, the dose and duration of exposure, and individual vulnerabilities.

### **Health Effects of Mercury Exposure**

Mercury's health impacts vary depending on its chemical form, with neurological and renal effects being the most consistently observed across all types.

*   **General Health Concerns**
    *   Mercury is one of WHO's top ten chemicals of major public health concern [WHO].
    *   Exposure can cause serious health problems, especially harming fetal development [WHO].
    *   Health effects span the nervous, digestive, immune systems, lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes [WHO].
    *   The health effects depend on the form of mercury, dose, duration, exposure route, age (unborn infants are most vulnerable), and individual health [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Neurological and renal toxicity are the most consistently observed health effects across all mercury forms [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
*   **Methylmercury Exposure (mainly from fish/shellfish)**
    *   **Neurological:** Harm to the brain and nervous system, especially in fetuses and young children [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury). Symptoms can include visual field loss, tingling, poor coordination, speech/hearing/walking impairments, and muscle weakness [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury). Prenatal exposure can affect brain development and cognitive/motor skills [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury). Developmental neurotoxicity (hyperactivity, impaired motor coordination, memory, sociability) and adult neurobehavioral effects have been observed [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Renal:** Nephrotoxicity with dose- and duration-dependent severity [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Cardiovascular:** Some evidence of blood pressure changes and altered cardiac function [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Immunological/Reproductive:** Potential immune stimulation and reduced fertility markers in susceptible animals [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Cancer:** Limited evidence of carcinogenicity in male rats (forestomach, thyroid) [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
*   **Elemental Mercury Exposure (vapor inhalation)**
    *   **Neurological:** Tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular issues, headaches, sensory disturbances, and impaired mental function [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury). Mood swings, irritability, nervousness, and timidity have also been reported [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Renal:** Reduced glomerular function and tubular injury have been reported [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Respiratory:** At high/fatal exposure, respiratory toxicity (pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, respiratory failure) is observed [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   **Other:** High exposure may damage kidneys, the respiratory system, and cause death [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
*   **Inorganic Mercury Salt Exposure**
    *   **Corrosive:** Inorganic mercury salts are corrosive [WHO].
    *   **Organ Damage:** Can cause kidney and other toxic effects, and damage the gastrointestinal tract and nervous system [WHO, EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   **Symptoms:** Skin issues, mood/memory disturbances, mental changes, and muscle weakness [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   **Other potential effects (in animals):** Cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive; some carcinogenic signals in male rats (forestomach, thyroid) [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
*   **Ethylmercury**
    *   Ethylmercury, found in thiomersal in some vaccines, is not considered a health risk [WHO].

### **Sources of Mercury Exposure**

Humans are primarily exposed to mercury through diet, especially fish, and inhalation of mercury vapor from industrial settings or broken products.

*   **Dietary Exposure**
    *   **Methylmercury:** The main exposure for most Americans is by eating fish and shellfish containing methylmercury [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury). Methylmercury builds up in fish, with higher levels in larger, longer-lived predator fish [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).
    *   **Inorganic Mercury:** Other foods may contain inorganic mercury [UK Gov](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mercury/statement-on-the-effects-of-mercury-on-maternal-health).
*   **Inhalation Exposure**
    *   **Mercury Vapor:** Humans are exposed mainly via inhalation of mercury vapor, particularly in industrial settings [WHO] and from using or breaking products that contain mercury [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).
    *   **Product Spills:** Inhalation of mercury vapor from broken containers or devices can be dangerous, especially in poorly ventilated indoor spaces [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury). Common household items like thermometers and certain jewelry pendants can release mercury if broken [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).
*   **Environmental Sources**
    *   Mercury is a naturally occurring element found in air, water, and soil [WHO].
    *   Coal burning is a major source of atmospheric mercury emissions [WHO].
    *   Microorganisms convert mercury into methylmercury in water and land [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).
*   **Historical and Current Product Use**
    *   Mercury compounds have been used in various products (fungicides, preservatives, antiseptics), though many uses have been discontinued [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).
    *   Some products still contain mercury, including those manufactured abroad or sold illicitly [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury). Examples include batteries, lamps, dental amalgam, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals [WHO].
    *   Elemental mercury from heritage uses (thermometers, measuring devices) also poses exposure risks [WHO].

### **Risk Management and Guidance**

Regulatory bodies provide guidelines and advice to minimize mercury exposure, particularly for vulnerable populations.

*   **Vulnerable Populations**
    *   Unborn infants and young children are most vulnerable to the effects of mercury [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Methylmercury crosses the placenta and blood-brain barriers, making embryo neurodevelopment and young children particularly susceptible [UK Gov](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mercury/statement-on-the-effects-of-mercury-on-maternal-health).
    *   Pregnant and breastfeeding women are highlighted as sensitive sub-populations [UK Gov](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mercury/statement-on-the-effects-of-mercury-on-maternal-health).
*   **Regulatory Guidelines and Tolerable Intakes**
    *   The UK government advises limiting certain fish consumption during pregnancy: no more than 2 portions of oily fish per week and no more than 2 tuna steaks per week; avoid shark, swordfish, marlin, raw shellfish, and uncooked/cured fish [UK Gov](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mercury/statement-on-the-effects-of-mercury-on-maternal-health). This advice keeps methylmercury exposure conservative relative to tolerable weekly intakes (TWIs) [UK Gov](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mercury/statement-on-the-effects-of-mercury-on-maternal-health).
    *   EFSA (European Food Safety Authority) 2012 TWIs are 1.3 µg/kg body weight for methylmercury and 4 µg/kg body weight for inorganic mercury [UK Gov](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mercury/statement-on-the-effects-of-mercury-on-maternal-health). Current UK population exposure (including pregnant women and fetuses) from food, water, soil, and air remains below these TWIs, indicating a low risk [UK Gov](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mercury/statement-on-the-effects-of-mercury-on-maternal-health).
    *   EPA sets maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) for inorganic mercury in drinking water to limit exposure, balancing health protection with feasibility [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
*   **Public Health Actions**
    *   Key action priorities include eliminating mercury mining, reducing its use in gold mining, promoting mercury-free and safer alternatives, preventing exposure from heritage uses, and managing mercury in products [WHO].
    *   WHO recommends eliminating mercury mining and reducing its use in artisanal and small-scale gold mining [WHO].
*   **Personal Safety Measures**
    *   Most people have trace amounts of mercury in their bodies, typically below levels of health concern [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).
    *   If concerned about mercury exposure, consult a physician or poison control (1-800-222-1222) [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Learn and follow proper cleanup steps for mercury spills from thermometers or broken devices [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).
    *   Be aware of products that historically contained mercury, including those manufactured abroad or sold illicitly [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/how-people-are-exposed-mercury).

Summary:

- Mercury effects span three chemical forms: elemental mercury, inorganic mercury salts, and methylmercury (implied under “three chemical categories”).
- Across all forms, the most consistently observed health impacts are neurological and renal effects in humans and animals.

Elemental mercury (vapor exposure):
- Neurological: tremor, vision and motor coordination impairment, cognitive deficits (memory, integrated function), mood/behavioral symptoms (mood swings, irritability, nervousness, timidity).

Inorganic mercury salts:
- Neurological and renal toxicity consistently observed in animal studies (oral exposure).

Methylmercury (implied under inorganic/other categories):
- Neurological: developmental neurotoxicity (hyperactivity, impaired motor coordination, memory, sociability); adult neurobehavioral effects (hyperactivity, impaired learning/memory) and overt neurotoxic signs in animals.
- Renal: nephrotoxicity with dose- and duration-dependent severity.
- Cardiovascular: some evidence of blood pressure changes and altered cardiac function.
- Immunological/Reproductive: potential immune stimulation and reduced fertility markers in susceptible animals.
- Cancer: limited evidence of carcinogenicity in male rats (forestomach, thyroid).

Epidemiological context:
- For elemental mercury: consistent neurological effects in exposed adults; some renal decrements.
- For methylmercury: data largely from fish/high fish diet exposures; cardiovascular and other systemic associations exist but are less consistently characterized across all populations.

- Neurological and renal toxicity are the most consistently observed health effects across mercury forms, with additional potential cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive, and carcinogenic findings mostly from animal studies or specific exposure contexts.

Summary:
- Mercury poisoning comes from exposure to elemental (Hg0) or inorganic mercury; inhalation is the main risk for elemental mercury, while ingestion is the main route for inorganic compounds.
- Key organs affected: central nervous system and kidneys; short-term exposure can cause nausea, vomiting, fever, muscle pains, cough, chest pain, and potential lung, kidney, liver, and muscle damage. Long-term inhalation can cause neurotoxicity (fatigue, tremor, headaches, depression, irritability, hallucinations) and kidney/mouth effects.
- Common sources: spills, workplaces (electrical/thermometer manufacturing, chemical plants, dental practices); do not vacuum mercury.
- Response steps:
  - Remove yourself from exposure and seek medical advice (call NHS 111, poison info service, or 999 if very unwell).
  - Skin: remove contaminated clothing; wash skin with soap and lukewarm water for 10–15 minutes.
  - Eyes: remove contact lenses; rinse with lukewarm water for 10–15 minutes.
  - Inhalation/ingestion: seek medical advice promptly.
- Small spills (e.g., broken thermometer): wear disposable gloves; carefully collect broken glass and droplets with sticky tape/paper into a double bag; do not wash contaminated items; ventilate room for 24 hours; avoid vacuuming; contact local environmental health for disposal.
- Large spills: contact local environmental health for guidance.
- Workplace safety: safe exposure levels are set below levels thought to cause harm to protect workers.

## Mercury Safety: A Team Report

**Introduction:**
Mercury is a naturally occurring element present in air, water, and soil, leading to some level of human exposure [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/]. This report summarizes the potential health risks associated with mercury exposure, common sources, and preventative measures based on the provided search results.

### Health Effects of Mercury Exposure

Exposure to mercury can lead to a broad range of serious health risks, particularly for fetal and early-life development. All forms of mercury (elemental, inorganic, and organic) can affect the nervous system and kidneys [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/], [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/], [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf].

*   **Neurological and Behavioral:**
    *   Neurological and behavioral disorders, tremors, cognitive/motor deficits, mood changes, learning and memory problems are consistently observed across various mercury forms [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/], [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/], [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf].
    *   Fetal and early-life exposure, especially to methylmercury, is particularly dangerous and can lead to neurodevelopmental concerns and birth defects [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/], [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/], [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf], [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio].
*   **Kidney Damage:**
    *   Mercury exposure can lead to decrements in kidney function, including tubular and glomerular damage [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/], [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/].
*   **Other Organ Systems:**
    *   **Immune System:** Immune stimulation has been observed in susceptible strains [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/], [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf].
    *   **Respiratory System:** Severe respiratory injury has been reported at high exposure to elemental mercury vapor, and irritation of respiratory pathways [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/], [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio]. Short-term exposure can cause cough and chest pain [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].
    *   **Digestive System:** Nausea and vomiting can occur with short-term exposure [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].
    *   **Cardiovascular System:** Possible increased blood pressure and altered cardiac function have been reported in human studies, though findings vary [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/], [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf].
    *   **Reproductive System:** Fertility impairment and reduced sperm quality have been noted in animals, and high exposures may increase the risk of spontaneous abortions [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/], [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio].
    *   **Skin and Eyes:** Skin problems can occur [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/].
*   **Cancer Risk:**
    *   The EPA considers mercuric chloride and methylmercury as possible human carcinogens. IARC classifies methylmercury as possibly carcinogenic, while inorganic/elemental mercury is not clearly classified or classifiable [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf]. Some evidence of carcinogenicity in male rats has been observed for inorganic mercury salts [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/].

### Common Sources of Mercury Exposure

Humans are exposed to mercury through various pathways, including environmental, occupational, and dietary sources.

*   **Dietary Exposure:**
    *   Methylmercury is primarily ingested from eating fish and shellfish, especially large predatory species like shark, swordfish, and giant mackerel [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/], [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio].
*   **Inhalation:**
    *   Elemental mercury vapor is a major source of exposure, often from industrial processes, coal burning, artisanal and small-scale gold mining, and spills [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/], [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].
*   **Occupational Exposure:**
    *   Workplaces involved in electrical/thermometer manufacturing, chemical plants, and dental practices pose risks [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].
*   **Consumer Products:**
    *   Sources include batteries, thermometers, fluorescent lamps, dental amalgams, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/], [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf].
*   **Prenatal/Lactation:**
    *   Mercury can be transmitted to the fetus and baby during pregnancy and breastfeeding [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio].

### Prevention and Safety Regulations

Preventing mercury exposure involves a combination of individual actions, public health guidance, and international cooperation.

*   **Dietary Recommendations:**
    *   Limit consumption of high-mercury fish, especially for pregnant women and children. Choose smaller fish species to reduce methylmercury exposure [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf], [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio].
    *   Follow state fish advisories [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf].
*   **In-Home Prevention:**
    *   Replace mercury-containing devices (e.g., thermometers, blood pressure monitors) with digital alternatives [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio].
    *   Avoid storing, handling, or burning liquid mercury [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio].
*   **Spill Response:**
    *   For small spills (e.g., a broken thermometer), wear disposable gloves, ventilate the room for at least 24 hours, and carefully collect broken glass and mercury droplets with sticky tape or stiff paper. Place collected materials in a double bag or a sealed jar. Do not use brooms or vacuum cleaners, as this can spread the mercury. Contact local environmental health for disposal guidance [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf], [https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio], [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].
    *   For large spills, contact local environmental health authorities [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].
*   **Medical Advice:**
    *   If mercury exposure is suspected, consult a healthcare professional immediately [https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxfaqs/tfacts46.pdf], [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].
*   **Policy and Global Action:**
    *   The Minamata Convention on Mercury aims to reduce global mercury emissions and exposures by eliminating mercury mining, promoting non-mercury gold-extraction techniques, and advocating for mercury-free medical devices and safer disposal [https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/].
    *   Regional initiatives, such as the ISLANDS Pacific Child Project, are developing legislative tools to manage mercury-containing products and enhance waste management [https://www.unep.org/gef/news-and-stories/technical-highlight/pacific-island-countries-advance-regional-action-mercury].
    *   Workplace safety regulations set exposure levels below those thought to cause harm to protect workers [https://pulseatlas.health/conditions/mercury-poisoning-occupational/].

Mercury is a toxic element found naturally in air, water, and soil. All humans have some exposure, mainly through inhaled mercury vapors from industrial processes and through eating fish containing methylmercury. Key health risks include damage to the nervous, digestive, immune systems, kidneys, lungs, skin, and eyes, with particular danger to fetal development in utero and early life. - Eliminate mercury mining and reduce its use in gold mining and other industries.
- Phase out mercury-containing products (thermometers, barometers, switches, lamps, dental amalgam) and promote mercury-free alternatives.
- Reduce mercury emissions from coal burning and industrial processes.
- Promote safer handling and disposal to prevent exposure.

runs.report:
# Is Mercury Safe? A One-Page Report for Our Team

Mercury is a toxic element with various forms that pose significant health risks to humans and the environment. All humans experience some level of exposure, primarily through consuming contaminated fish and inhaling mercury vapors. The safety of mercury depends heavily on its form, the amount of exposure, and individual vulnerabilities, with fetuses and young children being most susceptible.

## Health Risks of Mercury Exposure

Mercury poses a range of health risks, affecting multiple body systems depending on the form, dose, and duration of exposure.

*   **General Health Risks**
    *   Mercury is a neurotoxin and can damage the nervous, digestive, immune systems, kidneys, lungs, skin, and eyes [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Exposure can lead to motor and cognitive problems, mood changes, numbness, and skin rashes [NIEHS](https://www.niehs.nih.gov/health/topics/agents/mercury).
    *   Fetuses and young children are particularly vulnerable to mercury's toxic effects [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   If concerned about mercury exposure, individuals should consult a physician or poison control [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

*   **Methylmercury**
    *   Most exposure occurs through eating fish and shellfish contaminated with methylmercury, which accumulates up the food chain [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury), [NIEHS](https://www.niehs.nih.gov/health/topics/agents/mercury).
    *   High levels can harm the nervous system, leading to symptoms like loss of peripheral vision, tingling sensations, poor coordination, difficulties with speech, hearing, walking, and muscle weakness [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Prenatal exposure from a mother's fish consumption can impair fetal brain and nervous system development, affecting cognitive, memory, attention, language, motor, and visual-spatial skills [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

*   **Metallic (Elemental) Mercury**
    *   Exposure primarily occurs through inhaling mercury vapors, often from spills or broken products [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Symptoms can include tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular changes, headaches, sensory disturbances, and impaired cognitive test performance [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Very high exposures can lead to kidney problems, respiratory failure, or death [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   A few drops of liquid elemental mercury can contaminate indoor air, and skin contact allows absorption into the bloodstream [NIEHS](https://www.niehs.nih.gov/health/topics/agents/mercury).

*   **Inorganic Mercury**
    *   High exposures can damage the gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, and kidneys [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Symptoms may include skin rashes, mood and memory disturbances, mental changes, and weakness [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

*   **Ethylmercury**
    *   Ethylmercury, found in thiomersal used in some vaccines, is not associated with health risks [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

## Mercury Sources and Public Health Priorities

Mercury is found in many everyday products and industrial processes, necessitating global efforts to reduce exposure and promote safer alternatives.

*   **Common Sources and Products Containing Mercury**
    *   Mercury is naturally present in air, water, and soil [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   Common sources include batteries, measuring devices (thermometers, barometers), switches, lamps, dental fillings (amalgam), and some cosmetics and pharmaceuticals [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   Industrial processes, such as coal burning and gold mining, are significant contributors to mercury emissions [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

*   **Public Health Priorities**
    *   **Eliminate and Reduce Use:** Phasing out mercury mining, reducing its use in gold mining and other industries, and promoting mercury-free alternatives for products like thermometers, barometers, switches, lamps, and dental amalgam [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   **Reduce Emissions:** Decreasing mercury emissions from coal burning and industrial processes [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   **Safer Handling and Disposal:** Promoting safer handling and disposal practices to prevent exposure [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   **Healthcare Initiative:** India aims to eliminate mercury-containing medical devices from healthcare by 2030, with several regions already achieving mercury-free status in public health services. This includes strengthening safe mercury-waste management and ensuring access to reliable alternatives [WHO](https://www.who.int/india/news-room/detail/22-10-2026-push-to-eliminate-mercury-based-devices-in-health-care).

## Safety Guidelines and Regulations

Various national and international efforts are in place to manage and minimize mercury exposure.

*   **National Strategy for Safe Disposal of Mercury-Containing Lamps (Canada)**
    *   Canada has established a national framework for the safe management, disposal, and recycling of lamps containing mercury. This includes requirements for safe handling, storage, transport, treatment, and disposal to prevent mercury release, with compliance and enforcement mechanisms [National Strategy for Safe and Environmentally Sound Disposal of Lamps Containing Mercury Act (S.C. 2017, c. 16)](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/N-16.8/index.html).

*   **U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)**
    *   The DOE provides documents on the long-term management and storage of elemental mercury, covering aspects of handling, storage, and disposal [Energy.gov](https://www.energy.gov/em/long-term-management-and-storage-elemental-mercury).

*   **Drinking Water Regulations**
    *   Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) exist for drinking water to limit mercury exposure [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).

Here’s a concise summary of the essential points from the FAQ on NobelPrize.org:

- Purpose and establishment: Alfred Nobel’s will created prizes to honor those who confer the greatest benefit to humankind. The Nobel Prizes fund from Nobel’s fortune, invested in safe securities.
- First and ongoing awards: The first prizes were awarded in 1901 and have been awarded annually since, with gaps during World Wars I and II.
- Prize categories: Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, and Peace. Economics (Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel) was added in 1968 as a memorial prize.
- Prize sharing and scope: A Nobel Prize can be shared by up to three individuals; the Peace Prize may also be awarded to an organization.
- Posthumous awards: A prize cannot be awarded posthumously. If a laureate dies after the prize is announced, they may still receive it; prior rules allowed posthumous awards in some cases.
- Nomination process: Laureates must be nominated by eligible nominators; self-nomination is not allowed. Except for the Peace Prize, nominations are invitation-based and nominator criteria vary by awarding institution.
- Final decision: Each prize-awarding committee works to fulfill Nobel’s will, selecting those who have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.
- Nobel Day: December 10 marks the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death and the Nobel Prize presentation day.

If you want a more targeted summary (e.g., only on nomination, or only on prize categories), tell me which part you need.

Summary:
- The claim that no Nobel Prize exists for mathematics due to an affair between Alfred Nobel’s wife and a mathematician is false.
- Nobel never married; the “wife” theory has no evidence.
- Possible explanations Nobel gave no mathematics prize: his prizes targeted fields he cared about (physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace; economics added later), and mathematics was viewed as too theoretical to yield the direct practical benefits Nobel sought.
- Another factor: Sweden’s King Oscar II had already endowed a separate mathematics prize, influenced by mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler.
- In short, there is no verified reason tied to an affair; the omission is likely due to Nobel’s interests and the landscape of prizes at the time.

## Report on the 2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics

This report addresses the query regarding the 2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics, drawing from the provided search results.

### Absence of a Nobel Prize in Mathematics

The Nobel Prizes, established by Alfred Nobel's will, do not include a category for mathematics.
*   **Original Categories:** Alfred Nobel's will created prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, and Peace [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/).
*   **Economics Prize:** The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was added in 1968 as a memorial prize, not part of Nobel's original will [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/).
*   **Reasons for Omission:** There is no verified reason tied to an affair involving Alfred Nobel, as Nobel was never married. Possible explanations for the omission include Nobel's focus on fields with direct practical benefits and the existence of another mathematics prize already endowed by Sweden's King Oscar II [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/).
*   **Posthumous Awards:** Nobel Prizes cannot be awarded posthumously [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/).

### Prestigious Awards in Mathematics (Alternatives to the Nobel Prize)

While there is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics, several highly respected international awards recognize significant contributions to the field.

*   **Fields Medal:**
    *   Awarded every four years by the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) to 2–4 mathematicians under 40 years old [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_of_mathematics), [source](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Honours/FieldsMedal/).
    *   Recognizes both current achievements and promising future work [source](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Honours/FieldsMedal/).
    *   **2026 Recipients and Contributions (closest available year in search results):**
        *   **Yu Deng:** PDEs, Boltzmann equation, nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics [source](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Honours/FieldsMedal/).
        *   **John Pardon:** Symplectic geometry, virtual fundamental cycles and related topics [source](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Honours/FieldsMedal/).
        *   **Jacob Tsimerman:** Arithmetic and complex algebraic geometry, period maps, and Andre-Oort conjecture [source](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Honours/FieldsMedal/).
        *   **Hong Wang:** Harmonic analysis and geometric measure theory [source](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Honours/FieldsMedal/).
*   **Abel Prize:**
    *   Established in 2003, it is awarded by the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters, with support from the IMU and European Mathematical Society for committee nominations [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_of_mathematics), [source](https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/other-prizes).
    *   Often seen as akin to a Nobel for mathematics [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_of_mathematics).
*   **Wolf Prize in Mathematics:**
    *   Established in 1978, it was historically considered a Nobel-like prize for mathematics before the Abel Prize [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_of_mathematics).
*   **Chern Medal:**
    *   Awarded every four years to one mathematician at the ICM, recognizing lifetime achievement [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_of_mathematics), [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mathematics_awards).
*   **ICTP-IMU Ramanujan Prize:**
    *   An annual prize for researchers under 45 from developing countries [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mathematics_awards), [source](https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/other-prizes).
*   **Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics:** An international award recognizing leading mathematicians [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mathematics_awards).

Given that there is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics, the query regarding the 2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics winner's citation cannot be answered. The most relevant information regarding recent significant mathematical contributions comes from the Fields Medal, with its 2026 recipients and their respective fields of study listed above.

# 2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics: Committee Citations

This report summarizes information regarding the Nobel Prize in Mathematics and related awards, specifically addressing the 2025 prizes.

## Absence of a Nobel Prize in Mathematics

*   The Nobel Prizes, established by Alfred Nobel's will, are awarded in six categories: Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, Peace, and Economic Sciences (added later). Mathematics is not among these categories [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes), [https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-why-alfred-nobel-left-the-subject-out-of-his-famous-awards-the-truth-behind-the-love-rivalry-rumour-and-the-prestigious-prizes-that-recognise-mathematicians-today/photostory/134813902.cms), [https://vajiramandravi.com/current-affairs/nobel-prize-winners-2025/](https://vajiramandravi.com/current-affairs/nobel-prize-winners-2025/).
*   The exact reason for this exclusion is unclear, but a popular rumor linking it to a romantic rivalry involving Alfred Nobel is unsupported by evidence [https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-why-alfred-nobel-left-the-subject-out-of-his-famous-awards-the-truth-behind-the-love-rivalry-rumour-and-the-prestigious-prizes-that-recognise-mathematicians-today/photostory/134813902.cms).
*   A more cautious view suggests that mathematics might not have aligned with Nobel's stated aim of "greatest benefit to humankind" within the specific fields he chose, despite its undeniable indirect influence on science [https://timesofindia.indiatim](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-why-alfred-nobel-left-the-subject-out-of-his-famous-awards-the-truth-behind-the-love-rivalry-rumour-and-the-prestigious-prizes-that-recognise-mathematicians-today/photostory/134813902.cms).

- Nobel Prizes cover physics, chemistry, physiology/medicine, literature, peace; economics was added later.
- Mathematics was not included in Nobel’s will, and no documented reason explains why; the original categories reflect Nobel’s personal vision, not a ranking of disciplines.

- Nobel Prizes cover Physics, Chemistry, Physiology/Medicine, Literature, Peace; Economics was added later. Mathematics has no Nobel Prize because Nobel’s 1895 will specified only those five fields.
- The popular rumor that Nobel excluded math due to a romantic rivalry with a mathematician is unsubstantiated; Nobel never married, and the tale is not backed by reliable evidence.

- The article debunks popular Nobel myths, focusing on four main points:
  1) There is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics because Alfred Nobel’s will named prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature, and Peace (awarded in Oslo); Mathematics was not included, possibly viewed as too theoretical.
  2) Einstein won the Nobel Prize for the Photoelectric Effect (1921), not for relativity; some committee members opposed relativity, and the prize was administered as a “law” rather than a theory.
  3) Winston Churchill is often thought to have won the Nobel Peace Prize; in reality he received the Nobel Prize in Literature (1953) for his writings and speeches, though he was proposed for Peace.
  4) The Economics Prize is not in Nobel’s original will; it was established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank and is officially “The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel,” funded by the bank, not Nobel’s estate.
